notes: Historical card sets. Dates are ranges — never collapse to a single year. Survival: extant|fragmentary|documented|lost. Holdings are split by institution. Attributions carry roles and confidence. Genealogy is a typed edge list. missing_cards uses cards.json IDs (pentacles = historical coins). primary_purpose captures original intent; later_uses records functional shifts. v1.1: added Tang dynasty, Spanish naipes, Catelin Geoffroy, Etteilla, Golden Dawn pseudo-node; fixed RWS→Thoth genealogy edge; added missing_cards arrays; added primary_purpose/later_uses.

decks.name: Tang Dynasty Leaf Game
decks.date_basis: Referenced in a text attributed to Princess Tongchang during the reign of Emperor Yizong (859–873 CE). The word 'yèzǐ' (leaves) likely refers to paper cards. The game rules and card descriptions are partially preserved in later Tang and Song dynasty writings.
decks.missing_cards_notes: No physical cards survive. The game is known only from textual references.

structure.notes: Card count and structure unknown. Some scholars propose 30–40 cards with monetary or hierarchical denominations. No suit structure comparable to Mamluk or European playing cards is documented.

attributions.name: Tang Dynasty court
attributions.notes: Association with Princess Tongchang; game may have spread from court to wider use

decks.transmission_path: Possibly an ancestor of Chinese paper money games, eventually influencing Mahjong and Chinese domino traditions. The connection to Western playing cards via the Silk Road remains speculative and not established in mainstream playing card scholarship.
decks.iconography_notes: Unknown; no surviving images.
decks.significance: If the textual attribution is accurate, this is the earliest documented reference to a card game anywhere in the world — predating the Mamluk deck by roughly 500 years. The connection to the European playing card tradition is debated and unproven; it may represent an independent invention rather than a direct ancestor.
sources: Needham, Joseph. Science and Civilisation in China. Vol. 4, Part 1. Cambridge, 1962.
Lo, Andrew. 'The Game of Leaves: An Inquiry into the Origin of Chinese Playing Cards.' Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies, Vol. 63, 2000.
decks.genealogy_isolated_reason: Possible independent invention; the connection to European playing cards via the Silk Road is not established in mainstream playing card scholarship. Treated as a parallel lineage, not an ancestor.

decks.name: Mamluk Playing Cards
decks.date_basis: Style analysis and paper evidence; 1375 is the conventional midpoint citation

structure.notes: No trump suit — this is a pure pip deck. Direct ancestor of European playing cards via Moorish transmission.

decks.transmission_path: Entered Europe via Iberian peninsula and Italy c. 1370–1380; suits transformed into cups/coins/swords/clubs in Spain and Italy
decks.iconography_notes: No human figures by Islamic convention. Court cards use inscriptions naming the rank rather than depicting figures. Polo stick suit is direct ancestor of the wands/batons suit.
decks.significance: Earliest surviving multi-suit playing card set. The four-suit structure and 52-card count established the template for all European playing cards and eventually tarot.
sources: Dummett, Michael. The Game of Tarot. Duckworth, 1980.
Kaplan, Stuart R. The Encyclopedia of Tarot. Vol. I. U.S. Games Systems, 1978.
decks.missing_cards_notes: 15 of 52 cards survive. The Mamluk deck uses a different structure (polo_sticks, cups, swords, coins; 13 ranks; no trumps) so comparison to tarot IDs is not meaningful. The surviving cards include examples from multiple suits but are not mapped to the tarot card ID namespace.

decks.name: Spanish Naipes (earliest documented)
decks.date_basis: A 1371 Barcelona account book records the purchase of playing cards. The 1377 Basel chronicle of Johannes von Rheinfelden describes a 52-card game that reached Europe 'from the Saracens.' No physical cards from this period survive; the earliest surviving European cards are c. 1390–1430.
decks.missing_cards_notes: No physical cards from this specific date range survive. Documentary evidence only.

structure.notes: The four Latin suits (cups/coins/swords/clubs) are direct adaptations of the Mamluk suits (cups/coins/swords/polo sticks). Only 3 court cards per suit (no queen) — a feature of all Latin-suited decks. The queen appears only in northern European (German/French) variants.

attributions.name: Iberian cardmakers (Moorish transmission)
attributions.notes: The 1377 Basel chronicle explicitly states cards arrived 'from the Saracens' — i.e., via the Moorish presence in Iberia. The Latin suit system is a direct adaptation of the Mamluk suits.

decks.transmission_path: Mamluk Egypt → Iberian peninsula (Moorish transmission) → Italy and northern Europe. The Italian suit system (cups/coins/swords/clubs) derives from the Spanish. German and French suits (hearts/bells/leaves/acorns and hearts/diamonds/clubs/spades) are later regional adaptations.
decks.iconography_notes: The pole suit (Mamluk polo sticks) becomes clubs/batons in Iberian and Italian decks. The queen figure is absent — Mamluk and Latin-suited decks have king + two male officers. French decks later added the queen, creating the 52-card deck with four courts.
decks.significance: The documentary pivot between Mamluk Egypt and European playing cards. The Latin suit system established here (cups/coins/swords/clubs) remains the standard for Italian, Spanish, and Portuguese cards to this day — and is the direct ancestor of the tarot minor arcana suits.
sources: Dummett, Michael. The Game of Tarot. Duckworth, 1980.
Hargrave, Catherine Perry. A History of Playing Cards. Houghton Mifflin, 1930.
Mann, Sylvia. All Cards on the Table. Jonas, 1990.

decks.name: Charles VI Tarot
decks.date_basis: Named after erroneous 19th-century attribution to Charles VI of France. Stylistic analysis places it in Northern Italian workshops c. 1440–1470. The 1392 Charles VI court payment for 'painted cards' refers to different cards entirely.

structure.notes: Only 17 trump cards survive. Related stylistically to the Visconti-Sforza tradition but distinct workshop.

attributions.name: Northern Italian workshop
attributions.notes: Ferrara and Milan both proposed; unresolved

decks.commissioned_for: Unknown; entered French royal collections before 1800
decks.transmission_path: Entered French royal library; name Charles VI applied by mistake in 19th century
decks.iconography_notes: The Hanged Man is shown by the feet like the Visconti versions. The World shows a city inside a wreath. The Fool has a distinctive jester's motley. Related to but distinct from the Visconti-Sforza tradition.
decks.significance: Important witness to early Italian tarot iconography, independent of the Visconti commissions. The misattribution to Charles VI was repeated uncritically for over a century.
sources: Dummett, Michael. The Game of Tarot. Duckworth, 1980.
Huson, Paul. Mystical Origins of the Tarot. Inner Traditions, 2004.
decks.missing_cards_notes: Only 17 of 78 cards survive — all major arcana (trump cards). All 56 minor arcana are missing. Of the 22 trumps, 5 are also absent; the specific 17 surviving trumps are documented but the missing 5 have not been definitively identified against a canonical trump order.

decks.name: Visconti di Modrone Tarot
decks.date_basis: Heraldic evidence — Visconti–Savoy betrothal arms appear; Bianca Maria Visconti married Francesco Sforza in 1441; Filippo Maria died 1447

structure.notes: The earliest known tarot deck with 22 trump cards. Missing: The Devil, The Tower, The Star, The Moon, The Sun, The World, the Knight of Coins, and three pip cards.

holdings.institution: Brera Art Library (Biblioteca dell'Accademia di Brera)
Yale University's Cary Collection of Playing Cards

attributions.name: Filippo Maria Visconti
attributions.notes: Duke of Milan; arms on card backs

attributions.name: Bonifacio Bembo (attributed)
attributions.notes: Attribution based on stylistic comparison with Bembo's documented paintings; not documented in primary sources

decks.iconography_notes: The earliest tarot trumps. God the Father (The World) shows a nude figure in a mandorla. The Chariot is drawn by horses, not sphinxes — pre-Marseille iconography. The Wheel of Fortune has blindfolded Fortune turning the wheel.
decks.significance: The earliest surviving tarot set. Establishes the 78-card structure that endures to the present. The luxury vellum and gold leaf indicate tarot began as aristocratic entertainment, not divination.
sources: Dummett, Michael. The Game of Tarot. Duckworth, 1980.
Berti, Giordano, and Andrea Vitali. The Tarot of the Old Path. AGM, 2001.
decks.missing_cards_notes: 6 major arcana definitively absent: The Devil (15), The Tower (16), The Star (17), The Moon (18), The Sun (19), The World (21). Knight of Pentacles (pentacles-12, historically 'Knight of Coins') also missing. 4 pip cards unidentified — the specific cards are not established in the scholarly literature.

decks.name: Visconti-Sforza Tarot
decks.date_basis: Heraldic arms date the core commission to shortly after Francesco Sforza took Milan in 1450. Bianca Maria's baton device and the Sforza serpent support c. 1451–1453 for the main hand. Some cards likely added by a second workshop c. 1470s.

structure.notes: Missing: The Devil, The Tower, and two minor suit cards. The World shows a female figure in a garland rather than a mandorla — iconographic evolution from Visconti di Modrone.

attributions.name: Francesco Sforza
attributions.notes: Duke of Milan from 1450; Sforza arms on cards

attributions.name: Bianca Maria Visconti
attributions.notes: Her personal device (baton) appears prominently

attributions.name: Bonifacio Bembo
attributions.notes: Documented association with the Sforza court; style consistent with his signed works

attributions.name: Antonio Cicognara (attributed)
attributions.notes: Possible second hand on the six replacement cards made c. 1470s

decks.iconography_notes: The most reproduced historical tarot. The Strength card shows a woman with a lion (later standard). The Star shows a nude woman pouring water. The Wheel of Fortune shows a king crowning a rising figure. Heraldic imagery throughout reflects Sforza dynastic claims.
decks.significance: The most intact and widely reproduced pre-Marseille tarot. Standard reference point for Renaissance tarot iconography. The Morgan Library holding alone has been reproduced in dozens of facsimile editions.
sources: Kaplan, Stuart R. The Encyclopedia of Tarot. Vol. I. U.S. Games Systems, 1978.
Moakley, Gertrude. The Tarot Cards Painted by Bonifacio Bembo. NYPL, 1966.
Dummett, Michael. The Game of Tarot. Duckworth, 1980.
decks.missing_cards_notes: The Devil (major-15) and The Tower (major-16) are definitively absent — notably the two most 'dark' trump cards. Whether this reflects censorship, loss, or original omission is debated. 2 minor suit cards also missing but not specifically identified.

decks.name: Sola-Busca Tarot
decks.date_basis: Engraving style and costume details place it in the 1490s; Venice is most proposed location based on engraving tradition

structure.notes: Complete 78-card deck. Unique in depicting the pips (minor arcana) with narrative figures — a feature adopted 400 years later by Waite and Smith in the RWS. Major arcana use Roman military heroes (Nebuchadnezzar, Nimrod, etc.) rather than standard tarot archetypes.

attributions.name: Sola-Busca family
attributions.notes: Named after the Milanese family in whose collection it was held for centuries

attributions.name: Unknown Venetian engraver
attributions.notes: Style suggests Venetian workshop; no signature survives

decks.commissioned_for: Unknown; possibly alchemical or hermetic society
decks.transmission_path: Held by Sola-Busca family until late 19th century; Waite and Smith viewed photographs at the British Museum c. 1909
decks.iconography_notes: The first fully illustrated minor arcana. Pamela Colman Smith is documented to have viewed photographs of this deck at the British Museum around 1909, the same year she produced the Rider-Waite-Smith deck. Direct iconographic borrowings from the Sola-Busca minor arcana into the RWS are extensively documented.
decks.significance: The missing link between Renaissance engraving and modern tarot. Smith's borrowings from Sola-Busca minor arcana make this deck a hidden parent of the Rider-Waite-Smith — the most influential tarot ever printed.
sources: Farley, Helen. A Cultural History of Tarot. I.B. Tauris, 2009.
Decker, Ronald, Thierry Depaulis, and Michael Dummett. A Wicked Pack of Cards. St. Martin's Press, 1996.

later_uses.notes: Pamela Colman Smith used the Sola-Busca as a visual source for the RWS minor arcana. The deck's original purpose is unclear — possibly hermetic or alchemical, possibly gaming with esoteric overlay.

decks.name: Minchiate Fiorentine
decks.date_basis: The word 'minchiate' appears in Florentine records c. 1466. The 97-card structure is documented in a 1530s manuscript. Surviving printed decks are 17th–18th century.

structure.notes: 41 trumps vs. tarot's 22. Added trumps include the 12 zodiac signs, 4 elements (Fire, Water, Air, Earth), and expanded virtues. The Fool is unnumbered as usual. The Papessa and Empress are replaced with the Eastern Emperor and Western Emperor to avoid religious controversy.

holdings.institution: Various; printed editions survive in BnF and private collections

attributions.name: Florence
attributions.notes: Documented in Florentine tax and civic records from c. 1466 onward

decks.transmission_path: Remained primarily a Florentine game; spread to Rome and Tuscany; declined after 1800
decks.iconography_notes: The Papessa and the Empress replaced to avoid controversy. Zodiac signs as trumps is unique to Minchiate. The game was played with 4 players using all 97 cards.
decks.significance: Largest trump structure in the tarot family. Demonstrates that the 22-trump count was not fixed — regional games expanded and contracted the trump set. The zodiac trumps influenced later esoteric tarot symbolism.
sources: Dummett, Michael. The Game of Tarot. Duckworth, 1980.
Pratesi, Franco. 'Italian Cards: New Discoveries.' The Playing Card, Vol. 16–17.

decks.name: Tarot de Marseille (Geoffroy, 1557)
decks.date_basis: Catelin Geoffroy's name and the year 1557 appear on the surviving trump cards. This makes it the earliest *dated* and *signed* Tarot de Marseille Type I deck — predating the Dodal by 144 years.
decks.missing_cards_notes: Only the 22 trump cards survive. All 56 minor arcana are lost.

structure.notes: Type I Tarot de Marseille — the earlier of the two Marseille type traditions. The surviving 22 trumps show the iconography that will be standardized in later Marseille editions. Strength at VIII, Justice at XI.

attributions.name: Catelin Geoffroy
attributions.notes: Name and date (1557) appear on the surviving cards

later_uses.notes: Marseille-type decks repurposed for cartomancy from c. 1785 onward

decks.transmission_path: Part of the Lyonnaise cardmaking tradition. Lyon was the center of French playing card production in the 16th century. The Marseille iconography was codified here before the industry shifted south.
decks.iconography_notes: The 1557 Geoffroy is the earliest datable reference point for Marseille Type I iconography. It predates the Dodal (c. 1701) by nearly 150 years, confirming the Marseille tradition's continuous existence from the mid-16th century.
decks.significance: Proof that the Marseille iconographic tradition was established by 1557 at the latest. Anchors the Marseille tradition as a 16th-century phenomenon rather than a 17th-century one. The Dodal and Conver are refinements of a tradition already old by their time.
sources: Dummett, Michael. The Game of Tarot. Duckworth, 1980.
Depaulis, Thierry. 'Tarot, jeu et magie.' BnF exhibition catalogue, 1984.

decks.name: Tarot de Paris
decks.date_basis: Style analysis and cardmaking technique place the surviving fragments in Paris c. 1590–1620. Held at the Bibliothèque nationale de France. Represents the Paris cardmaking tradition between Geoffroy (1557) and Noblet (c. 1650).
decks.missing_cards_notes: Only 16 Major Arcana cards survive. All minor arcana are lost.

structure.notes: Marseille Type I iconography in Parisian manufacture. Shows the transfer of the Marseille tradition from Lyon to Paris in the late 16th century.

attributions.name: Unknown Parisian cardmaker
attributions.notes: No maker's mark survives on these fragments. Attribution to Paris based on style and materials.

decks.transmission_path: Part of the 16th-century transfer of playing card production from Lyon (Geoffroy) to Paris. The Paris cardmaking guilds adapted the Marseille Type I iconography to northern manufacture, producing the idiom that Noblet would later standardize.
decks.iconography_notes: Shows early Parisian interpretation of Marseille Type I trumps. Minor differences in figure proportions and costume details distinguish these from the Lyon Geoffroy and later Noblet traditions. The Fool appears without the usual dog — replaced by a figure biting his own leg.
decks.significance: Bridges the gap between the Lyon Geoffroy (1557) and the Paris Noblet (c. 1650). Confirms that the Marseille iconographic tradition reached Paris by c. 1600, establishing the city as a cardmaking center a generation before Noblet's better-documented production.
sources: Kaplan, Stuart R. The Encyclopedia of Tarot. Vol. I. U.S. Games Systems, 1978.
Depaulis, Thierry. 'Tarot, jeu et magie.' BnF exhibition catalogue, 1984.

decks.name: Tarot de Marseille (Noblet, c. 1650)
decks.date_basis: Jean Noblet was registered as a master cardmaker in Paris from 1648. The deck style is consistent with mid-17th century Parisian production. No explicit date appears on the cards.
decks.missing_cards_notes: 22 trump cards survive at the Bibliothèque nationale de France. All 56 minor arcana are lost. The surviving trumps are sufficiently complete to reconstruct the Marseille Type II iconography.

structure.notes: Marseille Type II — the later and more widely disseminated Marseille type, with Strength at XI and Justice at VIII. The Noblet is the earliest known exemplar of the Paris-pattern Marseille Type II, the tradition that Dodal and Conver would later standardize.

attributions.name: Jean Noblet
attributions.notes: Noblet's name appears on the surviving cards. He was registered as master cardmaker in Paris from 1648. This is the only deck securely attributed to him.

later_uses.notes: Jodorowsky and Camoin used the Noblet as one of their reference decks in restoring the 1761 Conver Marseille, comparing woodblock details across surviving exemplars.

decks.transmission_path: Jean Noblet worked in the Parisian cardmaking tradition that adapted the Marseille iconography for northern French manufacture. His deck is the earliest extant Paris-pattern Marseille, establishing the template that Dodal (Marseille, c. 1701) and Conver (Marseille, 1761) would later adopt and refine.
decks.iconography_notes: The Noblet establishes what will become canonical Marseille Type II: the Hanged Man's tree shows no roots (later Marseille standardized this detail), the Lovers shows three figures with Cupid overhead, and the Devil shows a distinctly hermaphroditic figure unlike Lévi's later Baphomet-influenced versions. The High Priestess (II) shows a papal tiara — later Marseille editions would soften this.
decks.significance: Earliest known exemplar of the Paris-pattern Marseille Type II, the most widely reproduced tarot tradition. Establishes the iconographic vocabulary that Dodal, Conver, and all subsequent Marseille printers would follow. Critical reference point for understanding the evolution from Marseille Type I (Geoffroy 1557) to Type II. The Jodorowsky/Camoin restoration consulted it directly.
sources: Kaplan, Stuart R. The Encyclopedia of Tarot. Vol. I. U.S. Games Systems, 1978.
Dummett, Michael. The Game of Tarot. Duckworth, 1980.
Jodorowsky, Alejandro and Camoin, Philippe. The Way of Tarot. Destiny Books, 2004.
Depaulis, Thierry. 'Le Jeu de Tarot: histoire et pratique.' BnF, 1984.

decks.name: Tarot de Besancon
decks.date_basis: First documented Besancon-type impressions from the mid-17th century; production continued into the 19th century. A regional tradition with many cardmakers, not a single originating impression.

structure.notes: The defining feature: trump II (La Papesse) replaced by Juno, trump V (Le Pape) replaced by Jupiter. All other cards follow the Marseille woodblock tradition. Substitution avoids Catholic clergy imagery for Protestant Swiss/German markets.

attributions.name: Besancon cardmakers (multiple)
attributions.notes: A tradition of production, not a single maker. Known cardmakers include Joseph Jerger and others in the Besancon and Swiss tradition.

decks.transmission_path: Marseille woodblock tradition → Swiss/Alsatian cardmakers → Besancon production → gaming in Swiss, German, and Alsatian markets
decks.iconography_notes: The Juno/Jupiter substitution for Papesse/Pope is the sole structural departure from the Marseille model. Juno typically holds a scepter and peacock; Jupiter holds a thunderbolt. Reflects the pragmatics of selling into Protestant markets.
decks.significance: The most geographically widespread Marseille variant. Documents how the tarot traveled and adapted to local religious and political contexts. The Juno/Jupiter substitution is the earliest documented intentional modification of trump iconography for market reasons — a precursor to modern 'themed' decks.
sources: Kaplan, Stuart R. The Encyclopedia of Tarot. Vol. 1. 1978.
Decker, Depaulis, Dummett. A Wicked Pack of Cards. 1996.
Depaulis, Thierry. Tarot, Jeu et Magie. BnF exhibition catalogue. 1984.

decks.name: Tarot de Marseille (Dodal)
decks.date_basis: Jean Dodal registered as cardmaker in Lyon by 1701; surviving examples dated on stylistic and printing grounds to c. 1701–1715

structure.notes: Complete 78-card Tarot de Marseille type I. The Dodal is now considered the most faithful surviving Type I Marseille deck. Restored from originals by Yoav Ben-Dov.

attributions.name: Jean Dodal
attributions.notes: Name and city appear on several of the 22 trumps

decks.transmission_path: Woodblock tradition from Milanese tarot via French cardmaking guilds; standardized Marseille iconography by c. 1650
decks.iconography_notes: Type I Marseille. The Papesse (High Priestess) wears a tiara. The Popess controversy suppressed in some later editions. The numbering places Strength at VIII and Justice at XI — opposite of Waite-Smith.
decks.significance: The most faithful surviving witness to the Tarot de Marseille Type I tradition. Basis for many modern Marseille reproductions. The Dodal restoration by Yoav Ben-Dov (CBD Tarot) is the most studied modern edition.
sources: Ben-Dov, Yoav. Tarot: The Open Reading. CreateSpace, 2013.
Jodorowsky, Alejandro, and Marianne Costa. The Way of Tarot. Destiny Books, 2009.

later_uses.notes: Etteilla (c. 1785–1789) adapted the Marseille-type deck for cartomancy. Court de Gébelin's 'Egyptian origins' essay (1781) created the intellectual context. Marseille decks were repurposed for divination; they were never designed for it.

decks.name: Tarot de Marseille (Conver, 1761)
decks.date_basis: Date appears printed on the ace of coins face: 'N. Conver M.re Cartier a Marseille 1761.' One of the few exactly dated Marseille impressions.

structure.notes: Type II Marseille. Strength at XI, Justice at VIII (standard Marseille ordering). The Papesse (II) and Pope (V) are present, distinguishing it from the Besancon variant.

later_uses.notes: Adopted by French cartomancers in the 19th century. Became the standard reference for Marseille occultists.
Used by Alejandro Jodorowsky and Philippe Camoin as the primary source for their 1997 restored Tarot de Marseille — the most influential modern Marseille restoration.

attributions.name: Nicolas Conver
attributions.notes: Named on the ace of coins. One of the rare directly attributed Marseille productions. Conver was a master cardmaker (maitre cartier) of Marseille.

decks.transmission_path: Conver 1761 → 19th-century French cartomancers → Jodorowsky/Camoin restoration (1997) → contemporary Marseille revival
decks.iconography_notes: Type II is distinguished from Type I by subtle but consistent iconographic refinements: cleaner linework, more standardized figure proportions, revised color conventions. The Conver is the definitive Type II exemplar.
decks.significance: The single most influential surviving Marseille impression. Jodorowsky and Camoin's 1997 restoration — the most widely used Marseille deck in contemporary practice — was based directly on the Conver 1761. Any student of the Marseille tradition is effectively studying Conver's hand, 263 years later.
sources: Kaplan, Stuart R. The Encyclopedia of Tarot. Vol. 1. 1978.
Jodorowsky, Alejandro and Camoin, Philippe. The Way of Tarot. 2004.
Decker, Depaulis, Dummett. A Wicked Pack of Cards. 1996.

decks.name: Grand Etteilla
decks.date_basis: Jean-Baptiste Alliette (pseudonym Etteilla — his name reversed) published his cartomantic system progressively: 'Manière de se récréer avec le jeu de cartes nommées tarots' (1783) established the theory; the redesigned deck 'Grand Etteilla' appeared 1789–1791.

structure.notes: Card order and imagery completely redesigned for cartomancy. Card 1 (the Querent) replaces The Fool as the card representing the reading subject. The trumps are renumbered and given pseudo-Egyptian names (following Court de Gébelin's false attribution). Etteilla introduced upright/reversed meanings, positional spreads, and dedicated cartomantic keywords — the mechanics that define modern tarot reading.

holdings.institution: Bibliothèque nationale de France and private collections

attributions.name: Jean-Baptiste Alliette (Etteilla)
attributions.notes: First professional tarot reader in recorded history. Developed the cartomantic reading system independently of — and prior to — the Golden Dawn tradition.

decks.transmission_path: Etteilla's system spread through French occult circles and formed the basis of parlor cartomancy practice. Marie-Anne Adelaide Lenormand — who read for Napoleon — was trained in this tradition. The system reached England and eventually influenced Waite's methodology even as Waite rejected the Egyptian iconography.
decks.iconography_notes: The deck inverts the Marseille imagery and adds 'Egyptian' symbols based on Court de Gébelin's fabricated etymology. The Querent card (Card 1) is an innovation with no precedent. The reversed card system — where a card dealt upside down has an opposite meaning — is Etteilla's invention and now universal in tarot practice.
decks.significance: The pivot deck. Before Etteilla, tarot was a card game that some people also used for fortune-telling with standard playing cards. After Etteilla, tarot was a purpose-built divination tool. The upright/reversed system, the spread positions, the Querent card, and the cartomantic keyword tradition are all Etteilla's inventions — not ancient Egyptian ones.
sources: Decker, Ronald, Thierry Depaulis, and Michael Dummett. A Wicked Pack of Cards. St. Martin's Press, 1996.
Farley, Helen. A Cultural History of Tarot. I.B. Tauris, 2009.
Place, Robert M. The Tarot: History, Symbolism, and Divination. Tarcher/Penguin, 2005.

decks.name: Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn — Esoteric Correspondences
decks.date_basis: The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn was founded in 1888 by Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers, William Wynn Westcott, and William Robert Woodman. The tarot attribution schema — pairing each Major Arcana with a Hebrew letter, a path on the Kabbalistic Tree of Life, a planet or zodiacal sign, and an element — was codified in the initiation manuscripts, primarily the 'Book T' (sub-figura LXXVIII), c. 1888–1896. No physical deck was produced.
decks.missing_cards_notes: This is not a physical deck. It is a body of manuscript attributions.

structure.notes: Not a physical deck. The Golden Dawn attribution schema maps all 78 cards to Kabbalistic, astrological, and elemental correspondences. This schema was the direct source for both Waite's RWS and Crowley's Thoth — making the GD corpus the hidden parent of all modern esoteric tarot. The key manuscript is 'Book T' (sub-figura LXXVIII).

attributions.name: Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers
attributions.notes: Primary author of the Grade Papers including 'Book T'

attributions.name: William Wynn Westcott
attributions.notes: Co-founder and Supreme Magus; contributed cipher manuscripts

decks.commissioned_for: Internal use by Golden Dawn initiates
decks.transmission_path: The GD manuscripts were never publicly published in their original form. They entered public knowledge through Israel Regardie's 'The Golden Dawn' (1937–1940) and Aleister Crowley's semi-public disclosures. Both Waite and Crowley implemented the system in their respective decks before Regardie's publication.
decks.significance: The invisible infrastructure of all modern esoteric tarot. The Golden Dawn's attribution schema — Hebrew letter + Tree of Life path + planet/zodiac + element — is implemented in every esoteric tarot deck from 1909 onward. It transformed tarot from a gaming deck and folk fortune-telling tool into a systematic magical instrument. Waite and Crowley are rivals in the same tradition, not innovators of independent systems.
sources: Regardie, Israel. The Golden Dawn. Llewellyn, 1937–1940.
Greer, Mary K. Women of the Golden Dawn. Park Street Press, 1995.
Decker, Ronald, and Michael Dummett. A History of the Occult Tarot. Duckworth, 2002.

decks.name: Oswald Wirth Tarot (1889)
decks.date_basis: Published 1889 by Oswald Wirth with the support of Stanislas de Guaita. Limited edition of 350 copies. Major Arcana only; full 78-card Wirth not published until 1926.
decks.missing_cards_notes: The 1889 publication was 22 Major Arcana only. Wirth designed the full 78-card deck but published it in 1926 (Le Tarot des imagiers du Moyen Age). This entry covers the 1889 edition.

structure.notes: Major Arcana only. Based on the Marseille trump sequence but overlaid with Kabbalistic, astrological, and Hebrew-letter attributions per Eliphas Levi's system. The Fool is unnumbered (0), positioned before The Magician (I).

later_uses.notes: Widely adopted by French occultists and cartomancers in the early 20th century.

attributions.name: Oswald Wirth
attributions.notes: Swiss-French occultist, freemason, and artist. Designed the deck as a visual compendium of Levi's tarot-Kabbala synthesis.

attributions.name: Stanislas de Guaita
attributions.notes: French Rosicrucian occultist who sponsored and guided the project. De Guaita provided the Kabbalistic framework.

decks.transmission_path: Marseille iconography + Levi Kabbalistic system → Wirth 1889 Major Arcana → French occultist tradition → partial influence on Rider-Waite-Smith → Wirth 1926 full deck
decks.iconography_notes: Wirth retained the Marseille compositions as structural foundation but inscribed each card with Hebrew letters, astrological glyphs, and Kabbalistic correspondences. The Fool is explicitly card 0. First deck where esoteric attributions are visually integrated rather than added in a companion text.
decks.significance: The bridge between the French occultist Marseille reinterpretation (Levi, de Guaita) and the English Golden Dawn tradition (Waite, Crowley). Wirth's visual language — Marseille structure with integrated Kabbalistic notation — was a direct precursor to the RWS approach. Waite knew Wirth's work; the Fool-as-zero treatment is the clearest shared marker.
sources: Wirth, Oswald. Le Tarot des imagiers du Moyen Age. 1926.
Decker, Depaulis, Dummett. A Wicked Pack of Cards. 1996.

decks.name: Tarot des Bohémiens (Papus, 1889)
decks.date_basis: Published as part of Gérard Encausse (Papus), 'Le Tarot des Bohémiens,' Paris, Carré, 1889. First edition with 22 Major Arcana plates drawn by Gabriel Goulinat.
decks.missing_cards_notes: The 1889 Papus publication contains 22 Major Arcana illustrations by Goulinat, adapted from Wirth's 1889 esoteric deck. A full 78-card deck was not produced; the Minor Arcana were treated theoretically rather than illustrated.

structure.notes: Only 22 Major Arcana illustrated. Papus treated the Minor Arcana as a numerical/Kabbalistic system rather than providing card art. The theoretical framework for all 78 is described in text but only the 22 trumps exist as visual objects.

attributions.name: Gérard Encausse (Papus)
attributions.notes: Published under the pen name Papus. Encausse was the leading French occultist of his generation, founder of the Martinist Order, and prolific author on Kabbalah and esoteric tarot.

attributions.name: Gabriel Goulinat
attributions.notes: Illustrated the 22 Major Arcana plates for the 1889 edition, adapting Wirth's esoteric imagery with additional Martinist symbolism.

decks.commissioned_for: Publication for the Martinist esoteric reading public
decks.transmission_path: Papus received Wirth's 1889 Major Arcana through his connections to the French Rosicrucian/Martinist milieu (Stanislas de Guaita commissioned both projects). He adapted and extended Wirth's visual symbolism in the context of his own Kabbalistic and astrological system, producing a parallel theoretical framework to the emerging Golden Dawn system in London.
decks.iconography_notes: The Goulinat plates closely follow the Wirth 1889 imagery but add additional Martinist and Kabbalistic details. The Chariot shows astrological glyphs not present in Wirth. The Magician (called 'Le Bateleur') retains the lemniscate hat brim introduced by Wirth. The High Priestess (called 'La Papesse') shows a more explicit Kabbalistic duality motif. The deck is also notable for placing Hebrew letter attributions prominently on each card — anticipating the GD's Book T format.
decks.significance: Represents the parallel French esoteric tarot tradition to the English Golden Dawn system — both produced in 1889, both drawing on Lévi's Kabbalistic correspondences, but developing distinct visual vocabularies. Papus's written system influenced French tarot practice for decades and introduced the idea of tarot as a complete esoteric encyclopedia to a wide popular audience. The 'Tarot des Bohémiens' framing — associating the cards with Romani culture as alleged transmitters of Egyptian wisdom — was already a well-established myth by 1889 but Papus systematized it most influentially.
sources: Encausse, Gérard (Papus). Le Tarot des Bohémiens. Carré, Paris, 1889.
Decker, Ronald; Depaulis, Thierry; and Dummett, Michael. A Wicked Pack of Cards. St. Martin's Press, 1996.
Farley, Helen. A Cultural History of Tarot. I.B. Tauris, 2009.

decks.name: Rider-Waite-Smith Tarot
decks.date_basis: Published by Rider & Company, London, December 1909. Copyright held by A.E. Waite; drawn by Pamela Colman Smith.

structure.notes: Coins suit renamed Pentacles. All 78 cards fully illustrated with narrative scenes — a direct departure from all prior pip-only minor arcana traditions. Strength at VIII, Justice at XI (reversed from Marseille). Fool assigned to 0.

holdings.institution: Widely distributed; original plates at University of London archives

attributions.name: Pamela Colman Smith
attributions.notes: Produced all 78 illustrations; paid a flat fee; name omitted from early editions — the 'forgotten artist' of the most famous tarot

attributions.name: Arthur Edward Waite
attributions.notes: Provided symbolic program and Golden Dawn correspondences; commissioned Smith under his direction

attributions.name: William Rider & Son
attributions.notes: Published December 1909

decks.transmission_path: Became the standard tarot in the English-speaking world after 1970s occult revival; copyright expired; now the most reproduced tarot structure in history
decks.iconography_notes: All pip cards (Ace–10 in each suit) given full narrative scenes — unprecedented in tarot history. Draws directly from Sola-Busca (confirmed) and Marseille. The Page of Cups fish image is lifted almost directly from a Sola-Busca card.
decks.significance: The defining tarot of the 20th and 21st centuries. Every modern deck is either a derivative or a deliberate departure from RWS. Smith's contribution was uncredited for most of the deck's existence; the name 'Rider-Waite' erased the artist.
sources: Farley, Helen. A Cultural History of Tarot. I.B. Tauris, 2009.
Greer, Mary K. Women of the Golden Dawn. Park Street Press, 1995.
Decker, Ronald, and Michael Dummett. A History of the Occult Tarot. Duckworth, 2002.

decks.name: The Pictorial Key to the Tarot
decks.date_basis: Published by William Rider and Son, London, in December 1910 — the same month as the Rider-Waite-Smith deck itself (December 1909 for the deck; the Key followed within a year). Waite wrote it as the authorised interpretive companion. The US edition appeared via Dodd, Mead & Co. simultaneously. It has remained in continuous print, most commonly via the University Books (1959) and later Weiser Books reprints.
decks.missing_cards_notes: Text document, not a physical deck. The companion reading guide to the Rider-Waite-Smith Tarot.

structure.notes: A prose treatise of approximately 340 pages organised around the 78 cards. Part I: 'The Veil and Its Symbols' — the Egyptian pseudo-history of tarot origins that Waite accepted from Court de Gébelin while privately acknowledging its uncertainty. Part II: 'The Doctrine Behind the Veil' — the esoteric symbolism of the Major Arcana. Part III: 'The Outer Method of the Oracles' — divination spreads and reading instructions for all 78 cards. Part IV: 'The Secret Tradition in Goëtia' — connecting tarot to Solomonic magic. The Major Arcana interpretations are famously evasive: Waite was bound by his Golden Dawn oath not to reveal the inner symbolic meanings, so the Key gestures toward the symbolism while deliberately not explaining it. This deliberate opacity is part of what drove Crowley to write The Book of Thoth as a counter-text — he had no such scruples about secrecy.

attributions.name: Arthur Edward Waite
attributions.notes: Waite's primary esoteric text on tarot; the authorised companion to the deck he designed with Pamela Colman Smith. Waite was a prolific occultist, co-founder of the Fellowship of the Rosy Cross, and a long-time member and eventual schismatic from the Golden Dawn. His approach was always Christian-mystical, not Thelemic or atheist, which accounts for the Key's pietistic tone and the deck's distinctive combination of Golden Dawn symbolism with accessible Christian imagery.

attributions.name: William Rider and Son
attributions.notes: Rider & Co. gave their name to the deck (Rider-Waite) in this period. They were a major occult publisher in Edwardian London.

decks.commissioned_for: General occult reading public; companion to the RWS deck
decks.transmission_path: Continuously in print since 1910. The University Books reprint (1959) and subsequent Weiser Books edition made it the standard reference for two generations of English-language tarot readers. It is the most-cited single tarot text in English and the interpretive foundation for virtually all RWS-tradition reading systems. Its silence on the deeper symbolism (by Golden Dawn oath) paradoxically made it more influential: readers projected their own meanings into the gaps, which is structurally why the RWS tradition produced the enormous diversity of modern deck interpretations.
decks.iconography_notes: Text-only in its original form. Later editions (University Books, Weiser) include black-and-white reproductions of Pamela Colman Smith's images. The text describes each card's design in detail, often emphasising what Waite calls 'the secret symbolism' while simultaneously withholding it. The Key is also the source of the famous error that has propagated into almost all English-language tarot: Waite misidentified the figure in The High Priestess as 'Isis' rather than the Shekinah or the Queen of the West — a conflation that has shaped 100 years of RWS interpretation.
decks.significance: The interpretive axis of all RWS-tradition tarot. Where The Book of Thoth is technically exhaustive and initiatory, the Pictorial Key is accessible and deliberately incomplete — which, paradoxically, made it more generative. It established the 78-card reading framework (Major → core psychological forces; Minor → circumstances and events) that all modern tarot teaching builds on. Together with the deck itself, it created the modern idea of 'tarot interpretation' as a practise distinct from cartomancy. Its counterpart-in-silence to The Book of Thoth defines the fundamental split in modern tarot philosophy: Waite's Christian mysticism vs Crowley's Thelemic initiation, accessible vs technical, gestural vs precise, devotional vs analytical.
sources: Waite, Arthur Edward. The Pictorial Key to the Tarot. William Rider and Son, 1910.
Decker, Ronald, Thierry Depaulis, and Michael Dummett. A Wicked Pack of Cards. St. Martin's Press, 1996.
Greer, Mary K. Women of the Golden Dawn. Park Street Press, 1994.

decks.name: Liber AL vel Legis (The Book of the Law)
decks.name_local: Liber Legis; The Book of the Law
decks.date_display: 1904 (received in Cairo, April 8–10); 1909 (first print, The Equinox Vol. 1 No. 1)
decks.date_basis: Aleister Crowley claimed to have received the text through his wife Rose Kelly (acting as medium) from an entity named Aiwass over three successive noons, April 8–10, 1904, in Cairo. The original manuscript in Crowley's handwriting survives at the Warburg Institute, London. Crowley published it in The Equinox, Vol. 1, No. 1 (March 1909). The date_earliest is 1904 (claimed reception); date_latest is 1909 (verifiable public record).
decks.missing_cards_notes: Text document: 220 verses in three chapters, each attributed to one of the Thelemic divine figures (Nuit, Hadit, Ra-Hoor-Khuit). Not a card deck. The original handwritten manuscript survives.

structure.notes: Three chapters, each attributed to a different divine voice: Chapter I — Nuit (the infinite sky, the body of the night, the principle of unlimited space). Chapter II — Hadit (the point within Nuit, the spark of consciousness, the complement of infinite space). Chapter III — Ra-Hoor-Khuit (the hawk-headed lord, the martial child of Horus, the active force of the current Aeon). Total text: approximately 9,000 words. The divine triad Nuit/Hadit/Ra-Hoor-Khuit directly determines the iconography of the Thoth Aeon card (major-20). Chapter I, verse 57 contains the line 'All these old letters of my Book are aright; but Tzaddi is not the Star' — the direct textual authority for Crowley's reassignment of Hebrew letters to The Star (major-17) and The Emperor (major-04) in the Thoth deck.

attributions.name: Aleister Crowley
attributions.notes: Crowley claimed the text was dictated by Aiwass, his Holy Guardian Angel and a preternatural intelligence, speaking through his wife Rose Kelly. The manuscript is undeniably in Crowley's handwriting. Whether 'dictated' means authored by Crowley's subconscious or by an external entity is theologically contested within Thelema and of no concern to card history. For genealogy purposes: Crowley is the text's effective author.

attributions.name: Rose Edith Kelly (later Rose Crowley)
attributions.notes: Rose Crowley (née Kelly, 1874–1932) identified the communicating entity as Horus/Ra-Hoor-Khuit after Crowley tested her with images in the Cairo Museum (she correctly identified the Stele of Revealing, inv. 666, without being shown it first). Her role in the Cairo Working is documented in Crowley's diaries and in subsequent Thelemic history.

decks.commissioned_for: Thelemic practitioners; the founding scripture of the Aeon of Horus
decks.transmission_path: Published in The Equinox Vol. 1 No. 1 (1909) with scholarly apparatus. Reprinted in multiple Crowley collections throughout the 20th century. Now in the public domain and freely available. The text is the foundational scripture of Thelema — functioning for Thelemites as the Torah, Bible, or Quran functions in older religious traditions. Its direct influence on the Thoth Tarot is twofold: (1) the three divine voices of Liber AL become the three figures on the Aeon card (Nuit/Hadit/Ra-Hoor-Khuit); (2) the cryptic instruction in I:57 'Tzaddi is not the Star' is Crowley's sole textual authority for his Hebrew letter reassignment in the Thoth system.
decks.iconography_notes: The text itself contains no images, but its iconographic impact on the Thoth deck is systematic. Nuit (Chapter I) is depicted as a great arching starry figure in the Thoth Aeon card and appears as background cosmology throughout. Hadit (Chapter II) appears as a winged solar disc. Ra-Hoor-Khuit (Chapter III) appears as the hawk-headed child god. The Stele of Revealing (Cairo Museum inventory 666) that triggered the Cairo Working contains an image of Ra-Hoor-Khuit receiving offerings — this image directly influenced the Thoth Aeon iconography. The Star card's reassignment of Tzaddi (I:57) also determined the visual restructuring: the Star receives the Heh attribution (window, sight, observation, revelation) which is why Harris painted the figure with a butterfly (Psyche — soul as observer).
decks.significance: The root text of the Thelemic system that generated the Thoth Tarot. Without Liber AL, neither the Aeon card nor the Tzaddi swap exists, and therefore the Thoth deck lacks its two most radical structural departures from all prior tarot. The text functions in this genealogy as the Steele Sermon does for the Marseille tradition — not a deck, but the document that most directly shaped what followed. The Cairo Working (April 8–10, 1904) that produced it is, from the perspective of card history, the founding event of Thelemic tarot: the moment when a received text rather than a designed system became the authority for card iconography. This makes Liber AL unique in the entire genealogy — no other deck has a founding scripture that explicitly dictates card assignments and iconographic elements by name.
sources: Crowley, Aleister. Liber AL vel Legis (The Book of the Law). The Equinox, Vol. 1, No. 1. London: Wieland, 1909.
Kaczynski, Richard. Perdurabo: The Life of Aleister Crowley. North Atlantic Books, 2010.
DuQuette, Lon Milo. Understanding Aleister Crowley's Thoth Tarot. Weiser, 2003.

decks.name: Thoth Tarot
decks.name_local: The Book of Thoth: A Short Essay on the Tarot of the Egyptians
decks.date_basis: Work commenced 1938; Lady Frieda Harris produced paintings 1938–1943 under Crowley's direction. Deck not published in Crowley's lifetime; first published 1969 by Grady McMurtry / O.T.O.

structure.notes: Court card hierarchy restructured. Coins renamed Disks. Strength renamed Lust (XI), Justice renamed Adjustment (VIII). The Fool assigned to 0. Projective geometry (Frieda Harris's system) underlies the visual structure.

attributions.name: Lady Frieda Harris
attributions.notes: Produced all 78 paintings; used projective geometry (inspired by Rudolf Steiner) as underlying visual system

attributions.name: Aleister Crowley
attributions.notes: Directed Harris according to his Thelemic and Kabbalah system; correspondence between them survives

decks.commissioned_for: Thelemic esoteric system; companion to The Book of Thoth text
decks.transmission_path: Published posthumously 1969; standard deck for Thelemic practitioners and a major influence on occult revival decks
decks.iconography_notes: The visual language is projective geometry — forms that appear to move and fold into each other. The Lust card (XI) depicts Babalon riding the Beast. The Fool is the most complex Fool card in any deck — an empty, boundless figure. Hebrew and astrological attributions are visible on card faces.
decks.significance: The second major axis of modern tarot after RWS. Where RWS is narrative and accessible, Thoth is geometric and initiatory. The two traditions split essentially all modern tarot into camps.
sources: Crowley, Aleister. The Book of Thoth. O.T.O., 1944.
DuQuette, Lon Milo. Understanding Aleister Crowley's Thoth Tarot. Weiser, 2003.

decks.name: The Book of Thoth
decks.name_local: The Book of Thoth: A Short Essay on the Tarot of the Egyptians
decks.date_basis: Written 1938–1944 in parallel with Harris's paintings. First published as a subscription edition of 200 copies by O.T.O. (Ordo Templi Orientis), 1944. Crowley died 1947. The Weiser Books reprint appeared in 1969 simultaneously with the first public edition of the Thoth Tarot deck.
decks.missing_cards_notes: No physical deck — a written treatise. The companion deck (thoth-tarot) was painted by Lady Frieda Harris 1938–1943 under Crowley's direction.

structure.notes: Not a deck. A written treatise of approximately 300 pages organised around the 78 cards plus introductory essays on Kabbalah, Thelema, astrology, numerology, and alchemy. Unique among tarot texts for its systematic I Ching correspondences assigned to each card — a synthesis never attempted by any prior tarot author. Structured as: Part One (general theory), Part Two (the trumps, one chapter per card), Part Three (the court cards), Part Four (the small cards), appendices on Gematria and the Tree of Life.

attributions.name: Aleister Crowley
attributions.notes: Crowley's most systematic tarot exposition; his final major work, written in his late 60s and early 70s during World War II. Integrates the complete Thelemic system he had developed across four decades (Liber 777, Equinox essays, Golden Dawn grade work).

attributions.name: O.T.O. (Ordo Templi Orientis)
attributions.notes: Limited subscription edition of 200 copies, 1944. The subscription price was high and access restricted to initiates. The Weiser reprint (1969) made it publicly accessible.

decks.transmission_path: Weiser Books reprint (1969) appeared simultaneously with the first public edition of the Thoth Tarot deck, establishing them as an inseparable pair. Now the authoritative reference for all Thoth-tradition tarot study. Cited in every serious Thoth commentary including DuQuette (2003) and Snuffin (2007). The text is the only source for Crowley's own interpretive framework; Harris's paintings cannot be fully decoded without it.
decks.iconography_notes: Text-only in original edition. Crowley describes each card's visual symbolism in detail, cross-referenced with Hebrew letters, astrological attributions, I Ching hexagrams, and Gematria values. Later Weiser editions occasionally include black-and-white card reproductions. The text reveals that several visual choices in the paintings encode specific Thelemic doctrines that are invisible to viewers unfamiliar with the system — the Lust card's golden cup, the Aeon's six-pointed star arrangement, the Fool's emptiness.
decks.significance: The most exhaustive single-author tarot commentary ever written, and the second axis of modern tarot theory after Waite's Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910). Where Waite was allusive and devotional, Crowley is technical and initiatory. Where Lévi sketched a Kabbalistic skeleton, Crowley built full architecture — integrating Western esotericism, Eastern (I Ching) systems, and Thelema into a unified divinatory grammar. The Book of Thoth establishes that the tarot is not a European folk tradition ornamented with occultism, but a formal language with grammar rules, and that reading the cards is an act of applied philosophy rather than intuitive pattern-matching.
sources: Crowley, Aleister. The Book of Thoth. O.T.O., 1944; Weiser Books reprint, 1969.
DuQuette, Lon Milo. Understanding Aleister Crowley's Thoth Tarot. Weiser, 2003.
Snuffin, Michael. The Thoth Companion. Llewellyn, 2007.
Kaczynski, Richard. Perdurabo: The Life of Aleister Crowley. North Atlantic Books, 2010.

decks.name: Sforza-Brambilla Tarocchi
decks.date_basis: Attributable on stylistic and heraldic grounds to the Sforza court under Ludovico Sforza ('il Moro', Duke of Milan 1494–1499) or the immediate post-Sforza Lombardy period. Iconographic style is later than the core Visconti-Sforza commission (c. 1451–1453). Associated with the Brambilla family collection that entered the Pinacoteca di Brera. Scholarly debate continues over whether this constitutes a distinct commission or displaced cards from the VS complex.
decks.missing_cards_notes: Approximately 48 cards survive in the Brambilla-Brera group, comprising major and minor arcana fragments. The precise count and the question of whether all surviving cards belong to a single commission are unresolved. Attribution as a separate commission from the VS proper remains debated.

structure.notes: Fragmentary. Standard 78-card Lombard tarot structure. Iconography follows the Bembo workshop tradition but with later Sforza heraldry and distinct treatment of certain trumps. The Wheel of Fortune shows four figures rather than three as in the earlier VS, consistent with a later workshop refinement.

attributions.name: Ludovico Sforza ('il Moro') — attributed
attributions.notes: Sforza heraldry on surviving cards points to the Sforza court c. 1491–1499. Attribution to il Moro specifically is speculative and contested.

attributions.name: Bembo workshop (attributed)
attributions.notes: Stylistic continuity with the Bonifacio Bembo tradition suggests related workshop production. Alternative attributions to other Lombard painters have been proposed; Bembo himself would have been elderly or deceased by this date.

decks.transmission_path: Held in Lombard noble collections → Brambilla family → donated to Pinacoteca di Brera
decks.iconography_notes: The Brambilla-Brera cards show stylistic evolution from the classic Visconti-Sforza: slightly more elongated faces, more elaborate background hatching, and more uniform gold leaf application — all consistent with a late-15th or early-16th century Lombard workshop. The Wheel of Fortune trump with four figures (vs. the VS three) and certain court card variations are the key iconographic markers distinguishing this group from the earlier VS commission.
decks.significance: If confirmed as a distinct commission, the Sforza-Brambilla group documents the continuation of luxury tarot production in the Lombard court after the main Visconti-Sforza commission — serving as a bridge between the painted Renaissance tradition and the early woodblock period. It is the least studied of the major early Lombard tarot groupings.
sources: Kaplan, Stuart R. The Encyclopedia of Tarot. Vol. I. U.S. Games Systems, 1978.
Dummett, Michael. The Game of Tarot. Duckworth, 1980.
Moakley, Gertrude. The Tarot Cards Painted by Bonifacio Bembo. NYPL, 1966.

decks.name: Jacques Viéville Tarot
decks.date_basis: Jacques Viéville is documented as a Paris master cardmaker registered with the guild between 1643 and 1664. The surviving deck is attributed to his workshop on typographic and stylistic grounds. The BnF holding is nearly complete but missing a small number of minor arcana. Contemporary with the Jean Noblet deck — both represent the Paris cardmaking tradition at its peak.
decks.missing_cards_notes: Approximately 72 of 78 cards survive in the BnF holding. All 22 major arcana are present. 6 minor arcana cards are absent; their specific identities are not documented.

structure.notes: Paris-tradition woodblock tarot with the most radical iconographic departures from the Marseille standard of any surviving pre-18th-century French deck. The Chariot is pulled by two right-facing horses (Marseille versions typically use left-facing sphinxes or horses). The Moon (La Lune) shows a haymaker harvesting grain in a pastoral landscape, completely replacing the Marseille crayfish-and-towers composition. Strength at VIII, Justice at XI.

attributions.name: Jacques Viéville
attributions.notes: Paris cardmaker registered with the guild 1643–1664. Style and maker's marks on the surviving cards support the attribution.

decks.transmission_path: Paris cardmaking guild → BnF acquisition → scholarly documentation; limited downstream influence compared to the Lyon/Marseille line
decks.iconography_notes: The Viéville is the most iconographically independent surviving pre-Marseille French tarot. Key departures: (1) La Lune shows a rural haymaker in a pastoral landscape — completely replacing the Marseille crayfish, dogs, and towers with no astronomical imagery whatsoever. (2) Le Chariot faces right with naturalistic horses rather than sphinxes. (3) La Tempérance pours from a single ewer rather than between two cups. (4) Le Mat is a bells-and-motley jester type. These departures suggest Viéville drew from a different Italian or Flemish model than the Lyon/Marseille cardmakers.
decks.significance: One of two major surviving Paris-tradition tarot decks (with the Noblet by Jean Noblet c. 1650). Together, the Noblet and Viéville document a Paris cardmaking tradition working contemporaneously with — but iconographically independent of — the Lyon/Marseille program. The Viéville's Moon card is the most anomalous trump image in any pre-esoteric tarot: a pastoral harvest scene with no celestial element. The reason for this iconographic substitution remains unexplained and is one of the open questions in early tarot scholarship.
sources: Depaulis, Thierry. Tarot, jeu et magie. BnF exhibition catalogue, 1984.
Decker, Ronald, Thierry Depaulis, and Michael Dummett. A Wicked Pack of Cards. St. Martin's Press, 1996.
Kaplan, Stuart R. The Encyclopedia of Tarot. Vol. I. U.S. Games Systems, 1978.

decks.name: Court de Gébelin — 'Du Jeu des Tarots' (1781)
decks.name_local: Le Monde Primitif analysé et comparé avec le monde moderne — Vol. VIII
decks.date_basis: Antoine Court de Gébelin published 'Du Jeu des Tarots' in Volume VIII of Le Monde Primitif, Paris, 1781. A second essay by the Comte de Mellet in the same volume introduced the Hebrew-letter-to-trump correspondence and the earliest published cartomantic spread method.
decks.missing_cards_notes: Not a physical deck. De Gébelin was writing about an existing Marseille-type deck, most likely a Type II similar to the Conver 1761. No new cards were produced.

structure.notes: Not a physical deck. De Gébelin's essay misidentified the Tarot de Marseille as an ancient Egyptian sacred book — 'The Book of Thoth' — brought to Europe by gypsies. Every element of this claim is false; the tarot is demonstrably 15th-century northern Italian. The Comte de Mellet's companion essay introduced the 22 trumps ↔ 22 Hebrew letters correspondence that would define Kabbalistic tarot for the next 200+ years.

attributions.name: Antoine Court de Gébelin
attributions.notes: Swiss-French Protestant pastor, Freemason, and amateur philologist. His Egyptian etymology is fabricated; his claim of ancient origins has been definitively refuted. He died in 1784.

attributions.name: Comte de Mellet
attributions.notes: Contributed a second essay in the same volume. De Mellet made the 22 trumps ↔ 22 Hebrew letters attribution — the single claim that drove all Kabbalistic tarot, from Etteilla through the Golden Dawn to Waite and Crowley.

later_uses.notes: Etteilla built his cartomantic system on de Gébelin's Egyptian claims from 1783. All subsequent esoteric tarot — Wirth, Golden Dawn, Waite, Crowley — inherits this foundation, even when rejecting Egyptian attribution specifically.

decks.transmission_path: 1781 publication → Etteilla (1783–1791) → Eliphas Levi Hebrew-letter synthesis (1855) → Golden Dawn manuscripts (1888) → Rider-Waite-Smith (1909) → Thoth Tarot (1938)
decks.significance: The single most consequential text in tarot history after the cards themselves. De Gébelin's fabricated Egyptian narrative transformed a 15th-century Italian card game into a purported ancient mystical codex. The misidentification is entirely wrong but extraordinarily generative: it produced Etteilla's cartomantic system, Levi's Kabbalistic synthesis, the Golden Dawn corpus, and ultimately Waite and Crowley. The entire tradition of esoteric tarot that dominates global practice today rests on de Gébelin's 1781 error.
sources: Court de Gébelin, Antoine. 'Du Jeu des Tarots.' Le Monde Primitif, Vol. VIII. Paris, 1781.
Decker, Ronald, Thierry Depaulis, and Michael Dummett. A Wicked Pack of Cards. St. Martin's Press, 1996.
Farley, Helen. A Cultural History of Tarot. I.B. Tauris, 2009.

decks.name: Grand Etteilla II (Lismon Edition)
decks.name_local: Grand Etteilla ou Tarots Égyptiens — édition Lismon
decks.date_basis: Jean-Baptiste Alliette (Etteilla) died in 1791. His Grand Etteilla (1789–1791) was subsequently pirated and republished by multiple Paris publishers. The 'Lismon' edition — attributed to publisher Simon Lismon — is dated c. 1826–1843 on typographic and engraving-style grounds. It is the most documented of the early Etteilla piracies.

structure.notes: Preserves Alliette's renumbered trump order and pseudo-Egyptian imagery. Card 1 (the Querent/Etteilla) remains the opening card. Upright and reversed cartomantic keywords printed directly on card faces — Alliette's innovation, retained in the Lismon. The Lismon introduces simplified redrawn figures compared to the original Alliette engravings, making it a distinct impression rather than a direct copy.

attributions.name: Simon Lismon
attributions.notes: Paris publisher active in the early-to-mid 19th century. The Lismon editions are the most studied of the early Grand Etteilla piracies.

attributions.name: Jean-Baptiste Alliette (Etteilla)
attributions.notes: The card numbering, keyword system, pseudo-Egyptian imagery, and reversed-meaning tradition are all Alliette's, reproduced without authorization after his death in 1791.

decks.transmission_path: Alliette Grand Etteilla (1789–1791) → Lismon piracy (c. 1826–1843) → 19th-century French cartomancy practice → basis of commercial French divination into the 20th century
decks.iconography_notes: The Lismon redraws several of Alliette's original engravings with simplified linework and updated Restoration-era costume details, but preserves the pseudo-Egyptian symbolic vocabulary (pyramids, ibis, and ankh-derived motifs) and the upright/reversed keyword pairs printed on card faces. The on-card printing of divinatory meanings — Alliette's invention — distinguishes the Etteilla tradition from all Marseille and Golden Dawn derivatives and anticipates the modern practice of 'keywords on cards'.
decks.significance: Documents the commercial transmisson of Alliette's cartomantic system after his death and demonstrates the commercial appetite for purpose-built divination decks in early 19th-century France. The Etteilla piracy market — multiple publishers reproducing and slightly altering the deck over fifty years — confirms that cartomancy had become a viable commercial category before the esoteric revival reached England. The Lismon edition is likely what 19th-century French cartomancers actually held in their hands.
sources: Decker, Ronald, Thierry Depaulis, and Michael Dummett. A Wicked Pack of Cards. St. Martin's Press, 1996.
Farley, Helen. A Cultural History of Tarot. I.B. Tauris, 2009.
Depaulis, Thierry. Tarot, jeu et magie. BnF exhibition catalogue, 1984.

decks.name: Cary Sheet
decks.date_basis: Paper watermark and woodblock stylistic analysis; compared against documented Milanese printer output of the period.
decks.missing_cards_notes: Single uncut printed sheet; not intended to represent a complete deck but a slice of production output.

structure.notes: Uncut woodblock-printed sheet containing 20 partial cards from a Milanese workshop. The earliest surviving evidence of mass-produced (as opposed to hand-painted luxury) tarot.

holdings.institution: Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University

attributions.name: Milanese printmaking workshop (unidentified)
attributions.notes: Stylistic features align with Lombard/Milanese woodblock tradition of the late 15th to early 16th century.

decks.transmission_path: Hand-painted Lombard tarocchi (Visconti-Sforza workshops) → woodblock mass production (Cary Sheet represents this transition) → Piedmontese/Savoyard cardmakers → Marseille tradition
decks.iconography_notes: Several cards on the sheet — notably The Moon (with a scene of astronomers or astrologers beneath a crescent) and The Star — prefigure Marseille Type II compositions by 200 years. The Cary Sheet is the single most important object for understanding the pictorial transition from aristocratic Visconti-Sforza hand-painting to the printed Marseille tradition.
decks.significance: The missing link between Lombard hand-painted tarocchi and the Marseille woodblock tradition. Before the Cary Sheet, scholars could only infer that woodblock tarot existed in the 16th century; this physical object proves it and shows the iconographic continuity — many of the compositional conventions later standardized in Marseille are already present.
sources: Dummett, Michael. The Visconti-Sforza Tarot Cards. George Braziller, 1986.
Kaplan, Stuart R. Encyclopedia of Tarot, Volume I. U.S. Games Systems, 1978.
Depaulis, Thierry. Early Italian Engraving and the History of the Tarot. 2013.

decks.name: Tarocchino Bolognese (Mitelli)
decks.name_local: Tarocchino di Bologna — Giuseppe Maria Mitelli
decks.date_basis: Dated against Mitelli's other engraving work for the Bentivoglio family; the Tarocchino plates bear his characteristic signature style and circulate in documented 1660s Bolognese inventories.
decks.missing_cards_notes: The 62-card tarocchino structure omits pip cards 2–5 of each suit entirely (16 cards removed from the standard 78); this is the game's defining structural feature, not a loss.

structure.notes: Bolognese tarocchino structure: 22 trumps + 40 numeral+court cards (ace, 6–10, page, knight, queen, king per suit). The 2s, 3s, 4s, and 5s of all four suits are permanently removed. Still played today in Emilia-Romagna as the game 'tarocchino bolognese'.

attributions.name: Giuseppe Maria Mitelli
attributions.notes: Bolognese painter and engraver (1634–1718), court artist to the Bentivoglio family. Signed several plates. His Tarocchino is the single most artistically ambitious surviving 17th-century tarot.

attributions.name: Bentivoglio family
attributions.notes: The Bolognese Bentivoglio nobles commissioned the engraved plates as a luxury presentation object. Mitelli's stylistic allegiance to the Bentivoglio is well-documented across his oeuvre.

decks.transmission_path: Visconti-Sforza Lombard tradition → Bolognese regional adaptation (removal of 2–5 pips, rise of tarocchino game) → Mitelli 1664 engraved edition → continuing Bolognese production into the 19th and 20th centuries → modern Dal Negro tarocchino editions
decks.iconography_notes: Mitelli's engravings are Baroque in composition — figures are three-dimensional, dynamic, and classically posed, departing radically from the flat woodblock tradition of Marseille. The trump sequence shares the Italian A/B ordering family but incorporates Bolognese-specific features: four 'Moors' (Mori) replace the Pope, Popess, Emperor, and Empress in later 18th-century printings to comply with Church censorship. The Mitelli edition pre-dates that substitution and preserves the full religious/imperial trump set.
decks.significance: The key surviving object for the Bolognese tarocchino tradition — a structurally distinct 62-card game that developed in parallel with (and independent of) the 78-card Marseille/Milan tradition. The tarocchino proves that by the mid-17th century tarot was already branching into regionally-structured games, not just regionally-styled art. The game is still played in Emilia-Romagna today, making this the longest continuous living tarot tradition.
sources: Dummett, Michael and John McLeod. A History of Games Played with the Tarot Pack. Edwin Mellen Press, 2004.
Depaulis, Thierry. Tarot, jeu et magie. BnF exhibition catalogue, 1984.
Bertozzi, Marco. Giuseppe Maria Mitelli: L'Invenzione del Tarocchino Bolognese. 2012.

decks.name: Lévi — Dogme et Rituel de la Haute Magie
decks.name_local: Éliphas Lévi — Dogme et Rituel de la Haute Magie
decks.date_basis: Documented publication dates: Dogme (1854–1855), Rituel (1856); republished together as a single work in 1861 with minor revisions.
decks.missing_cards_notes: Textual corpus with embedded woodcut illustrations, not a printed deck. Included illustrations for several Major Arcana (notably The Magician, The Chariot, and the famous Baphomet figure associated with The Devil).

structure.notes: Theoretical corpus assigning the 22 Major Arcana to the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet and to the 22 paths of the Kabbalistic Tree of Life. No printed deck was issued during Lévi's lifetime; the system was implemented in card form only after his death (Wirth 1889, Golden Dawn 1888–1900, Waite 1909).

decks.technique: Letterpress printing; woodcut illustrations including the original Baphomet drawing

attributions.name: Éliphas Lévi (Alphonse Louis Constant)
attributions.notes: French occultist (1810–1875), former Catholic seminarian, defrocked for socialist sympathies. His Kabbalah-tarot synthesis was autodidactic but systematized existing strands of de Gébelin, Court de Mellet, and Jewish Hermetic traditions.

decks.transmission_path: De Gébelin/de Mellet 1781 (Egyptian-origin + Hebrew-letter suggestion) → Lévi 1854–1856 (systematic 22-trump ↔ 22-letter assignment + tree-of-life mapping) → Papus, Wirth, Stanislas de Guaita (French adoption 1889) → Mathers, Westcott, Waite, Crowley (Golden Dawn and derivatives, 1888 onward) → all 20th and 21st century esoteric tarot
decks.iconography_notes: Lévi's Baphomet illustration — a seated goat-headed figure with human torso, torch between horns, and inscribed forearms — became the template for The Devil (card XV) in essentially every post-1875 esoteric tarot. The image does not come from any prior tarot; Lévi invented it synthesizing medieval templar mythology with Hermetic symbolism. His woodcut of The Chariot (with sphinxes) similarly shaped later depictions. Lévi did not illustrate all 22 trumps, but his textual descriptions fixed the interpretive framework.
decks.significance: The single most influential text in the history of esoteric tarot. Lévi's systematic assignment of the 22 trumps to Hebrew letters and Kabbalistic paths is the foundation on which the Golden Dawn, Wirth, Papus, Waite, and Crowley all built. Every esoteric deck since 1875 carries Lévi's fingerprints. Without this book, de Gébelin's 1781 suggestion would have remained a fringe curiosity; with it, tarot became a central component of modern Western occultism. This is the missing node between the 1781 French speculation and the 1888 Golden Dawn systematization.
sources: Lévi, Éliphas. Dogme et Rituel de la Haute Magie. Paris: Germer Baillière, 1854–1856.
McIntosh, Christopher. Eliphas Lévi and the French Occult Revival. SUNY Press, 1972.
Decker, Ronald and Michael Dummett. A History of the Occult Tarot 1870–1970. Duckworth, 2002.

decks.name: Paul Christian — Histoire de la Magie
decks.name_local: Jean-Baptiste Pitois (Paul Christian) — Histoire de la Magie
decks.date_display: 1863 (Histoire de la Magie); 1870 (L'Homme Rouge des Tuileries)
decks.date_basis: Documented first-edition publication dates: Histoire de la Magie (1863, Paris: Furne), L'Homme Rouge des Tuileries (1863, republished 1870).
decks.missing_cards_notes: Textual corpus — no printed deck issued.

structure.notes: Introduced the now-standard terminology 'arcanes majeurs' and 'arcanes mineurs' (Major / Minor Arcana) — the first documented use of these terms in any language. Framed the 22 trumps as 22 stations of an Egyptian mystery-initiation rite.

attributions.name: Jean-Baptiste Pitois (pen name: Paul Christian)
attributions.notes: French occultist and Napoleonic-era archivist (1811–1877). Worked under Charles Nodier at the Bibliothèque de l'Arsenal; claimed access to occult manuscripts that he almost certainly invented or embellished.

decks.commissioned_for: Popular occult readership / Second Empire Paris
decks.transmission_path: Lévi 1854–1856 (Kabbalistic framework) → Paul Christian 1863 (Egyptian initiation framing + Major/Minor Arcana terminology) → Papus 1889 (Tarot des Bohémiens adopts both framings) → Golden Dawn manuscripts (adopt Major/Minor terminology) → Waite 1909 / all later tarot literature
decks.iconography_notes: Christian provided no deck illustrations but described in prose an elaborate Egyptian initiation-temple where a novice walks past 22 allegorical wall-paintings corresponding to the 22 trumps. This Egyptian-pyramid framing is pseudo-historical — there is no archaeological or textual basis for it — but its vivid narrative shaped how Waite (subway temple metaphor) and later popular writers imagined the origin of tarot.
decks.significance: Invented the terminology 'Major Arcana' and 'Minor Arcana' that every subsequent tarot tradition adopted without credit. Also the source of the 'Egyptian initiation temple' frame that pervades popular tarot writing from 1890 onward. A node the Golden Dawn and Waite both implicitly depend on but rarely cite — Paul Christian is the hinge between Lévi's Kabbalism and the English-language tarot revival.
sources: Christian, Paul. Histoire de la Magie, du Monde Surnaturel et de la Fatalité. Paris: Furne, 1863.
Christian, Paul. L'Homme Rouge des Tuileries. Paris: Dentu, 1863.
Decker, Ronald and Michael Dummett. A History of the Occult Tarot 1870–1970. Duckworth, 2002.

decks.name: Tarot 1JJ (Swiss)
decks.date_basis: Müller & Cie company records and surviving early printings; the '1JJ' name derives from the ace of coins / Juno/Jupiter substitution convention established in the 1820s–1830s.
decks.missing_cards_notes: Complete 78-card deck; still in continuous production by AGMüller (Neuhausen am Rheinfall, Switzerland) as of the 21st century.

structure.notes: Complete 78-card Marseille-descended structure with two Protestant-market substitutions: card II (La Papesse) replaced by JUNON (Juno) and card V (Le Pape) replaced by JUPITER. Hence the name '1JJ' — J for Juno and J for Jupiter.

decks.technique: Initially woodblock; later chromolithograph; now offset print

attributions.name: Johannes Müller (Müller & Cie)
attributions.notes: Founded card-making firm in Schaffhausen, Switzerland, 1828. The company later moved to Neuhausen am Rheinfall and still operates as AGMüller.

decks.transmission_path: Tarot de Besançon (Protestant French-Swiss border tradition, c. 1650–1850, Juno/Jupiter substitutions) → Müller 1JJ Swiss adaptation (c. 1831 onward, standardized Juno/Jupiter + minor Swiss-style redrawings) → continuous AGMüller production to present day
decks.iconography_notes: The 1JJ Swiss preserves the Besançon classical-mythology substitutions (JUNON with peacock for La Papesse; JUPITER with eagle and thunderbolt for Le Pape) and applies 19th-century Swiss printing conventions: cleaner linework, flat color fills, printed titles in Roman type rather than blackletter. The remainder of the trump sequence and all 56 minors follow Marseille Type II iconography with minor Swiss-workshop simplifications.
decks.significance: The living descendant of the Protestant Tarot de Besançon tradition and one of the few continuously-printed tarots with direct 19th-century lineage. The 1JJ Swiss remained the dominant Swiss and German-speaking tarot for divination throughout the 20th century, predating the RWS export into German-speaking markets. Demonstrates how religious censorship (the Juno/Jupiter substitution) became permanent market differentiation — the 1JJ is still sold today even in Catholic markets, where its substitutions are no longer necessary.
sources: Kaplan, Stuart R. Encyclopedia of Tarot, Volume II. U.S. Games Systems, 1986.
Depaulis, Thierry. Tarot, jeu et magie. BnF exhibition catalogue, 1984.
AGMüller company history documentation.

decks.name: B.O.T.A. Tarot (Paul Foster Case)
decks.name_local: Builders of the Adytum Tarot — Paul Foster Case / Jessie Burns Parke
decks.date_basis: First publication by the Builders of the Adytum organization, Los Angeles, CA; Case founded B.O.T.A. in 1922 but the tarot was published in its definitive line-art form 1929–1931.
decks.missing_cards_notes: Complete 78-card deck, still published in its original uncolored form by the Builders of the Adytum to this day.

structure.notes: Full 78-card structure following RWS organization (Strength at VIII, Justice at XI; English suit names: Wands/Cups/Swords/Pentacles). Published as uncolored line drawings with an instruction booklet guiding students to color the cards themselves according to specific Qabalistic correspondences.

decks.technique: Uncolored line drawing (students color with prescribed watercolor palette)

holdings.institution: Various private collections and library holdings worldwide

attributions.name: Paul Foster Case
attributions.notes: American occultist (1884–1954), former stage magician, founder of Builders of the Adytum (B.O.T.A.) in Los Angeles. Former Alpha et Omega member (an Isis-Urania Temple Golden Dawn offshoot). Departed to form his own American esoteric tradition.

attributions.name: Jessie Burns Parke
attributions.notes: American illustrator who executed the line drawings under Case's direction, adapting Pamela Colman Smith's RWS compositions for the B.O.T.A. curriculum.

decks.transmission_path: Golden Dawn curriculum (manuscripts c. 1888–1900) → Alpha et Omega (post-Mathers GD fragment) → Case's American departure (1920s) → B.O.T.A. curriculum and deck (1929–1931) → continuous American esoteric tradition to present day
decks.iconography_notes: The B.O.T.A. cards are line-art derivatives of the RWS compositions with several doctrinal modifications reflecting Case's revisions to the Golden Dawn system. The most significant changes: some Hebrew letter attributions differ from Waite's (Case reassigns The Emperor from Heh to Tzaddi and The Star from Tzaddi to Heh, following a proposed Aleister Crowley-era swap that Waite rejected). The intentional uncoloring of the cards is pedagogical: students learn esoteric color correspondences by coloring the cards themselves according to B.O.T.A. instructions.
decks.significance: The primary American esoteric tarot lineage — distinct from both the English Golden Dawn (via Waite/RWS) and from Crowley's Thelemic Thoth tradition. Case rebuilt the Golden Dawn system from American first principles, and the B.O.T.A. deck is the material expression of that rebuild. Its influence on 20th-century American esotericism — especially through its correspondence-course pedagogy — is substantial but under-documented compared to RWS and Thoth. This deck is the major post-RWS node in the English-language esoteric tradition.
sources: Case, Paul Foster. The Tarot: A Key to the Wisdom of the Ages. Macoy Publishing, 1947.
Clark, Rachel. Paul Foster Case: His Life and Works. Limitless Light Press, 2013.
Decker, Ronald and Michael Dummett. A History of the Occult Tarot 1870–1970. Duckworth, 2002.

decks.name: Rosenwald Sheet
decks.date_basis: Stylistic dating by Kaplan and others places the three uncut woodblock sheets in the decade around 1500. Acquired by Lessing J. Rosenwald and donated with his print collection to the National Gallery of Art, Washington DC in 1943.
decks.missing_cards_notes: Three uncut woodblock sheets survive: one trump sheet (incomplete — appears to show ~19 of 22 trumps), one sheet with cups and coins, one sheet with swords and batons.
