Together they form most but not all of a 78-card tarot deck; no court-rank information is fully reconstructible.

structure.notes: Three-sheet layout suggests the intended deck was a complete 78-card Italian tarot, though the preserved sheets are incomplete. Card order on the trump sheet is significant evidence for the canonical Milanese trump sequence.

decks.material: Woodblock-printed uncut sheets on rag paper

attributions.name: Unknown Italian (Florentine or Emilian) printshop
attributions.notes: Attribution to Florence is commonly proposed on iconographic grounds; some scholars argue for Bologna or Ferrara based on figure conventions.

decks.transmission_path: Italian woodblock printing tradition (c. 1450–1500) → Rosenwald workshop sheets → commercial distribution (cards cut from sheets and played) → preservation of master sheet by collector → Rosenwald → NGA.
decks.iconography_notes: The trump sheet preserves a trump order closely matching the Steele Sermon canonical list, confirming the Milanese trump sequence was stable by c.1500. The pip cards show the Italian-suited conventions (batons, cups, swords, coins) with rank-specific ornamental patterns.
decks.significance: The Rosenwald and Cary sheets are the two primary witnesses to mass-produced 15th c. Italian tarot. Together they document that by c.1500 tarot had transitioned from luxury hand-painted decks (Visconti-Sforza, PMB) to commercial woodblock production, and they preserve the canonical Milanese trump order in printed form.
sources: Kaplan, Stuart R. Encyclopedia of Tarot. Vol. I. U.S. Games Systems, 1978.
Dummett, Michael. The Game of Tarot. Duckworth, 1980.
National Gallery of Art, Washington DC — Rosenwald Collection records.

decks.name: Steele Sermon (De ludo cum aliis)
decks.name_local: Sermones de ludo cum aliis — anonymous Franciscan manuscript
decks.date_basis: Paleographic dating of the manuscript to late 15th c.; Robert Steele published the transcription in 1900. The sermon is catalogued as BL Additional MS 5197 / also preserved in a Würzburg manuscript.
decks.missing_cards_notes: This is a manuscript document, not a deck. It is included in the corpus because it is the earliest complete written record of the 22 trump cards in canonical order, and therefore constitutes primary evidence for the structure of the trump sequence that all later decks inherit.

structure.notes: Records only the 22 trumps in a specific order: Bagatella, Empress, Emperor, Popess, Pope, Temperance, Love, Chariot, Fortitude, Wheel, Hunchback/Hermit, Hanged Man, Death, Devil, Tower, Star, Moon, Sun, Angel/Judgment, Justice, World, Fool. The ordering differs from later Tarot de Marseille convention.

attributions.name: Anonymous Franciscan preacher
attributions.notes: Sermon style and moralizing tone suggest a Franciscan friar in Northern Italy, preaching against gambling and the use of cards. Identity unrecovered.

decks.transmission_path: Late 15th c. Italian religious manuscript culture → preserved in monastery/institutional libraries → 19th c. British Library and Würzburg holdings → Steele 1900 transcription → central citation in all modern tarot historiography.
decks.iconography_notes: The manuscript describes no images but lists the 22 trumps by name in a specific sequence, which is the earliest surviving structural evidence for a canonical trump order. The sequence is designated 'Order A' by Dummett and represents the Milanese/Bolognese ordering tradition.
decks.significance: The Steele Sermon is the single most important textual witness to the structure of tarot before 1500. Without it, we would not know the canonical trump order existed this early or what form it took. Every later Marseille, RWS, and Thoth ordering can be traced back to the Order A sequence this manuscript preserves.
sources: Steele, Robert. 'A Notice of the Ludus Triumphorum and Some Early Italian Card Games.' Archaeologia 57 (1900): 185–200.
Dummett, Michael. The Game of Tarot. Duckworth, 1980.
Depaulis, Thierry. 'Early Italian Lists of Tarot Trumps.' The Playing-Card 36 (2007).

decks.name: Pierpont-Morgan Bergamo Tarot (PMB)
decks.date_basis: Distinct from the main Visconti-Sforza deck (c.1450–1480) on stylistic and heraldic grounds. Six cards are 17th c. replacements. Main surviving set dated on iconographic comparison with late Bembo workshop and post-Bembo Milanese painting.
decks.missing_cards_notes: PMB preserves 74 of 78 cards across three institutions. Six of the 74 (the Devil, Tower, Fortitude, Star, Moon, Sun — contested) are generally considered later 17th c. replacements painted to fill gaps. Historical literature sometimes conflates PMB with Visconti-Sforza; Dummett and Kaplan treat them as a distinct deck.

structure.notes: Full 78-card Italian tarot structure. Trump ordering and iconography follow the Milanese tradition, with Bembo-workshop stylistic conventions distinguishable from the slightly earlier Visconti-Sforza deck.

decks.material: Hand-painted on heavy cardstock with gold leaf and silver leaf backgrounds
decks.technique: Tempera and gold leaf on paper/cardstock (luxury commission)

attributions.name: Bembo workshop circle (post-Bonifacio Bembo)
attributions.notes: Style is consistent with the extended Bembo workshop tradition in Cremona and Milan, slightly later than the master-period Visconti-Sforza cards.

attributions.name: Unknown 17th c. painter
attributions.notes: Six cards considered later replacements, painted in a recognizably post-Renaissance style to complete the deck after original cards were lost.

decks.transmission_path: Bembo workshop (Cremona/Milan, c.1480–1510) → Sforza or Colleoni family inheritance → Colleoni palace Bergamo → 19th c. dispersal (sale of 35 cards eventually to Pierpont Morgan, New York; 26 to Accademia Carrara; 13 retained at Casa Colleoni).
decks.iconography_notes: Iconographically similar to Visconti-Sforza but distinct in painterly execution: figures are slightly more elongated, drapery conventions later, backgrounds more consistently gold-leafed. The replacement cards show unmistakable 17th c. academic painting conventions.
decks.significance: PMB is the third surviving luxury Visconti-era tarot (with Visconti di Modrone and Visconti-Sforza). Together these three decks document that hand-painted tarocchi production in Milan continued at the highest level for at least 60 years (c.1441–1510) across three distinct commissions, establishing tarot's court-art status before the transition to woodblock mass production.
sources: Kaplan, Stuart R. Encyclopedia of Tarot. Vol. I. U.S. Games Systems, 1978.
Dummett, Michael. The Game of Tarot. Duckworth, 1980.
Morgan Library & Museum catalogue MS M.630.

decks.name: Ferrara / Este Court Tarocchi
decks.name_local: Tarocchi della corte estense di Ferrara
decks.date_basis: Este court account books at Modena document payments for 'carte da trionfi' to Ferrara cardmakers in the 1450s–1470s. Surviving fragments attributed to the Este court on stylistic and heraldic grounds.
decks.missing_cards_notes: Only a small number of Este-attributed cards survive, split between Yale University Art Gallery (Cary Collection) and Museo Civico in Ferrara. No complete deck from the Este commissions survives.

structure.notes: Reconstructed as a standard 78-card Italian tarot. Surviving fragments suggest the Ferrarese iconographic tradition differed in detail from Milanese (different figure treatments, distinctive Este heraldry on court cards).

decks.material: Hand-painted on cardstock with gold and silver ground
decks.technique: Tempera on paper with metal leaf (luxury)

attributions.name: Ferrara court painters (Cosmè Tura circle, tentative)
attributions.notes: Some cards have been tentatively associated with the Tura/Del Cossa painterly environment that produced the Schifanoia frescoes, though no firm documentary link exists.

decks.patron: Este court (Borso d'Este and/or Ercole I d'Este)
decks.transmission_path: Este court commissions (Ferrara, c.1460–1480) → court dispersal through Este succession → fragmentation across Italian noble collections → 19th–20th c. acquisition by Yale Cary Collection (New Haven) and Museo Civico (Ferrara).
decks.iconography_notes: Ferrarese tarocchi stand as a third regional tradition alongside Milan (Visconti/PMB) and Bologna (later Mitelli lineage). The surviving fragments show distinctive Este heraldic elements and painterly conventions linked to the Schifanoia fresco cycle, pointing to a Ferrara-based court workshop separate from the Milanese Bembo tradition.
decks.significance: Establishes Ferrara as a third major 15th c. tarot production center alongside Milan and Bologna. The Este court commissions prove that tarot was not a monolithic Milanese phenomenon but a cross-regional aristocratic craft with distinct local iconographic traditions — a fact obscured when only the more fully surviving Visconti material is considered.
sources: Kaplan, Stuart R. Encyclopedia of Tarot. Vol. I. U.S. Games Systems, 1978.
Dummett, Michael. The Game of Tarot. Duckworth, 1980.
Bellosi, Luciano. 'Per la storia delle carte da gioco ferraresi.' Prospettiva, various numbers.

decks.name: Tarot de Marseille (Pierre Madenié, Dijon, 1709)
decks.name_local: Tarot de Marseille — Pierre Madenié, Dijon 1709
decks.date_basis: The deck bears a printed 1709 date on the Deux de Coupe and is signed 'Pierre Madenié à Dijon.' Among the earliest dated complete Tarot de Marseille Type II decks.
decks.missing_cards_notes: Several near-complete exemplars survive in Swiss and French collections. Restored for modern publication by Yves Reynaud.

structure.notes: Canonical Tarot de Marseille Type II structure: 22 trumps with Justice at VIII and Strength at XI, Papesse at II and Pape at V, French titles on trumps, Italian-style pip suits. The direct typographic ancestor of Dodal and Conver.

decks.material: Woodblock-printed cards, hand-stenciled color on cardstock

holdings.institution: Swiss Museum of Playing Cards (Schweizerisches Spielkartenmuseum)

attributions.name: Pierre Madenié
attributions.notes: Dijon master cardmaker, active early 18th c. His deck is signed and dated, giving it unusual dating certainty among Marseille-tradition decks.

decks.transmission_path: Paris-region Marseille tradition (Noblet 1650) → Dijon adaptation (Madenié 1709) → direct typographic influence on Marseille/Dodal (c.1701–1715) and Conver (1761) → modern Marseille restoration (Camoin-Jodorowsky 1997) → contemporary facsimile tradition (Reynaud, Flornoy).
decks.iconography_notes: The Madenié 1709 is the earliest clearly dated survivor of the Type II Tarot de Marseille iconographic canon. It standardizes the imagery that Dodal and Conver would propagate: the specific mountain-and-sun pattern on the Moon, the double cords on the Hanged Man, the specific crayfish on the Moon, the two dogs, and dozens of other micro-details that distinguish Type II from Noblet's Type I.
decks.significance: Madenié 1709 is the single most important dated node for the Tarot de Marseille canon. It proves the Type II iconography was fully stabilized by 1709, decades earlier than often assumed, and provides the documentary anchor for the Marseille tradition that Conver 1761 then propagates into global recognition. Without Madenié, the Noblet → Conver jump has no dated middle term.
sources: Depaulis, Thierry. Tarot, jeu et magie. BnF, 1984.
Reynaud, Yves. Tarot de Marseille de Pierre Madenié (Dijon 1709) — restoration edition.
Dummett, Michael and Ronald Decker. A History of the Occult Tarot 1870–1970. Duckworth, 2002.

decks.name: Ancien Tarot de Marseille (Grimaud / Paul Marteau, 1930)
decks.name_local: Ancien Tarot de Marseille — Grimaud (Paul Marteau recoloration)
decks.date_basis: Paul Marteau's recolored Tarot de Marseille was published by B.P. Grimaud in 1930. The line drawings are adapted from the 18th c. Marseille tradition (particularly the Conver 1761 and Dijon-lineage decks).
decks.missing_cards_notes: Continuously in print since 1930; probably the most-printed tarot deck of the 20th century prior to the rise of RWS-tradition decks in the English-speaking world.

structure.notes: Standard Tarot de Marseille Type II structure (Justice VIII, Strength XI, Papesse II, Pape V). Distinctive Marteau color palette: strong primaries, large blocks of flat color, characteristic Grimaud 'orange' pip backgrounds.

decks.material: Commercial printed cards on cardstock with Grimaud back pattern
decks.technique: Offset printing with stabilized color palette

attributions.name: Paul Marteau
attributions.notes: French occultist and Grimaud editor (1885–1966). His 1930 recoloration stabilized the Marseille palette for the 20th c. commercial market. His 1949 book 'Le Tarot de Marseille' became the standard French-language Marseille reference.

attributions.name: B.P. Grimaud
attributions.notes: Major French card publisher (Paris). The Grimaud Marseille became the de facto standard Marseille deck from 1930 until Jodorowsky's Camoin restoration in 1997.

decks.transmission_path: Conver 1761 and Dijon-lineage Marseille woodblock tradition → Paul Marteau's 1930 recoloration for Grimaud → continuous French commercial print run → 20th c. occult and cartomantic use in Europe → superseded in connoisseur/restoration use by Camoin-Jodorowsky 1997.
decks.iconography_notes: Line drawings follow 18th c. Conver-lineage closely but color palette is Marteau's 20th c. recalibration: stronger reds and yellows, consistent flat blue backgrounds, simplified blocks of color. The orange pip-card background is a Grimaud signature. Aesthetically the Grimaud differs noticeably from the 18th c. pochoir decks; this aesthetic shaped 20th c. expectations of 'what a Marseille looks like' in France.
decks.significance: The Grimaud-Marteau Marseille is the deck of 20th c. French cartomancy. Every mid-century French reader (Kardec-era spiritualists, surrealists in their divination moods, 1970s esotericists) used this deck. Marteau's 1949 'Le Tarot de Marseille' book paired with it became the dominant French tarot reference until Jodorowsky. The deck established the commercial-Marseille aesthetic that persisted until the Camoin-Jodorowsky restoration challenged its color choices in 1997.
sources: Marteau, Paul. Le Tarot de Marseille. Arts et Métiers Graphiques, 1949.
Depaulis, Thierry. Tarot, jeu et magie. BnF, 1984.
Jodorowsky, Alejandro and Philippe Camoin. The Way of Tarot. Destiny Books, 2009.

attributions.name: David Palladini
attributions.notes: American illustrator (1946–2020) in Art Nouveau and Art Deco idioms. Later also designed the Neo-Classical Tarot and The Linweave Tarot. His Aquarian was his first and most influential deck.

decks.transmission_path: RWS iconographic tradition (1909) → American 1960s–70s occult revival → Palladini's stylized Art Nouveau/Deco recomposition (1970) → dominant 'mod' tarot aesthetic in 1970s U.S. → influence on post-RWS indie deck designers.
decks.iconography_notes: Strict RWS compositional fidelity for the Minor Arcana (Smith's scenes preserved) but with Palladini's Art Nouveau linework and Deco stylization. The trumps show more invention: the figures are more stylized and less narrative than Smith's, with a characteristic flat-color-block aesthetic that became widely imitated. This deck is often the first tarot deck 1970s and 80s Americans encountered outside the classic RWS.
decks.significance: The Aquarian Tarot marks the beginning of the 'post-RWS art deck' era: a deck that is recognizably a RWS descendant but with a distinct artist's vision and aesthetic, not a pedagogical or esoteric retool. Every indie illustrated deck of the 1980s–2020s descends from this precedent of treating the tarot as a vehicle for a personal artistic idiom.

attributions.name: Godfrey Dowson
attributions.notes: British occultist-artist (1923–2005), long-time student of the Golden Dawn material. His Hermetic Tarot is the product of decades of study of GD ritual documents and the Waite-era Golden Dawn literature.

decks.commissioned_for: Advanced Golden Dawn practitioners and esotericists
decks.transmission_path: Golden Dawn ritual papers (c.1888–1900) → Waite/Crowley 20th c. commentaries → Regardie's publication of the Golden Dawn corpus (1937–1940) → Dowson's synthetic reconstruction of the ritual imagery into a complete deck (1979) → adoption by post-Regardie GD-tradition study groups.
decks.iconography_notes: The Hermetic is the single most informationally dense tarot ever produced: each card bears Hebrew letters, zodiacal and planetary sigils, Sephiroth attributions, elemental attributions, decan associations, and densely worked symbolic imagery drawn from the Golden Dawn ritual papers. It makes no concession to visual approachability; it is a ritual document in card form.
decks.significance: The Hermetic Tarot is the most faithful surviving visual transcription of the Golden Dawn ritual symbolic system. Where RWS (Waite) and Thoth (Crowley) each made editorial decisions that departed from the GD originals in different directions, Dowson attempts a pure synthesis: 'what would the Golden Dawn cards have looked like if the system itself drew them?' It is the scholarly-reference companion to the Thoth and the RWS for the Golden Dawn tradition.

structure.notes: 78-card structure but circular cards (not rectangular). Court cards renamed: Daughter/Son/Priestess/Shaman replacing Page/Knight/Queen/King. Orientation on circular cards is continuous, allowing subtler gradations of 'reversal' than binary upright/reversed.

decks.material: Circular commercial printed cards, color illustration

attributions.name: Karen Vogel
attributions.notes: American artist and feminist spirituality researcher; primary illustrator of the Motherpeace deck.

attributions.name: Vicki Noble
attributions.notes: American feminist spirituality writer and teacher; co-designer of the deck and author of the accompanying Motherpeace book (1983).

decks.transmission_path: Second-wave feminist spirituality movement (1970s) → archaeological goddess-civilization research (Gimbutas, Stone) → Vogel-Noble Berkeley collaboration (1978–1981) → commercial publication by U.S. Games Systems (1983) → defining artifact of 1980s–90s feminist tarot tradition → major influence on 2000s–2020s indie-deck wave.
decks.iconography_notes: Circular cards with no fixed orientation — a structural departure from every prior tarot. Imagery draws on reconstructed pre-patriarchal goddess iconography (Minoan, Catalhöyük, Old European), Native American and African religious imagery, and reimagined tarot archetypes centered on female figures and matriarchal reference points. Court cards rebuilt around priestess/shaman/daughter/son axes rather than king-queen-knight hierarchy.
decks.significance: Motherpeace is the founding document of feminist tarot and arguably of the entire post-RWS indie-deck era. It proves that the tarot structure (78 cards, 22 trumps, 4 suits) can carry a symbolic system radically different from the medieval-Christian-patriarchal framework it grew up in. Every indie deck that reframes tarot through a new cultural or political lens (queer, Afrofuturist, decolonial, ecological) is working in the Motherpeace lineage.

genealogy.notes: Mamluk four-suit structure transmitted via Iberian and Italian card-making tradition; tarot added the 22-trump layer on top of the inherited suit structure
Both Lombardy court commissions; shared iconographic conventions; Visconti-Sforza is more complete and better documented
Independent Northern Italian workshop working from same iconographic tradition
Marseille iconography descends from Lombardy tarot via Piedmontese cardmakers in the 15th–16th century. The woodblock standardization flattened and simplified the aristocratic originals.

Waite explicitly redesigned against the Marseille tradition, restoring what he believed were older esoteric correspondences. He kept the card order and structure while remaking the iconography entirely.
Pamela Colman Smith viewed photographs of the Sola-Busca at the British Museum c. 1909. The narrative pip card concept and specific compositions are demonstrably borrowed.

Crowley explicitly designed Thoth as a rival to and correction of Waite's deck — he called Waite's instructions 'deliberately misleading.' Both descend from Golden Dawn manuscripts, but Crowley's Thelemic system departs fundamentally from Waite's Christian mysticism.
Both expand on the same Lombard-derived trump structure. Minchiate added trumps; tarot proper stayed at 22.

The Charles VI deck (actually c. 1440–1470, Northern Italy) inherits the four-suit playing card structure from the Mamluk/Iberian tradition, then layers tarot trumps on top — same path as the Visconti decks but from an independent workshop.

The 'Charles VI' deck (Northern Italian, c. 1440–1470) represents an iconographic lineage that fed into the Marseille standardization. The Marseille Type I is a synthesis of multiple Northern Italian workshop traditions, not solely the Visconti-Sforza line.

Waite was a member of the Golden Dawn (Isis-Urania Temple). The RWS implements the Golden Dawn attributions: Hebrew letter↔trump, planet/zodiac↔trump, elemental↔suit. Smith was also a member. The GD manuscript 'Book T' is the direct source for Waite's symbolic program.

Crowley was a Golden Dawn initiate (Neophyte → Adeptus Minor). The Thoth deck implements the same GD attribution schema as RWS but extends it with Thelemic attributions. The key difference: Crowley restores Strength to VIII and Justice to XI (reversing Waite's swap back to Marseille order).

Etteilla's system of reading all 78 cards as a coherent cartomantic whole — with positional meanings, reversal meanings, and a spread system — became the template for all subsequent English-language tarot reading. Waite's 'Pictorial Key to the Tarot' (1910) is a direct descendant of Etteilla's reading methodology even as it rejected his 'Egyptian' iconography.
The Mamluk four-suit structure transmitted to the Iberian peninsula via Moorish contact. Spanish naipes are the direct European adaptation — cups, coins, swords, and polo sticks become batons/clubs.
The Italian suit system (cups/coins/swords/clubs) derives from the Iberian naipes, which in turn derive from the Mamluk deck. The tarot minor arcana suits are the naipes suits, unchanged.

The Catelin Geoffroy 1557 Marseille Type I is the earliest dated witness to the woodblock tradition that descends from Northern Italian (specifically Milanese/Piedmontese) cardmakers adapting the Visconti-era iconography for mass production.

Both are Type I Tarot de Marseille from the Lyonnaise cardmaking tradition. The Geoffroy 1557 establishes the iconographic standard that the Dodal (c. 1701) continues and refines. 144 years separate them; the visual program is consistent.
Conver 1761 is the Type II culmination of the Marseille woodblock tradition that begins with the Geoffroy 1557 (Type I). 204 years of continuous cardmaking in the Lyonnaise/Marseillaise tradition.
Both are Marseille productions from the same woodblock tradition. Dodal (c. 1701) is Type I; Conver (1761) is Type II. Type II refines Type I iconography without structural change.
Waite explicitly rejected the Marseille unillustrated pip tradition. The Conver 1761 — the definitive Type II Marseille — is among the specific decks he was reacting against.
The Besancon variant descends directly from the Marseille woodblock tradition. The Juno/Jupiter substitution is the only structural departure; all other iconography follows the Marseille program.
Contemporary productions from the same Marseille woodblock tradition. Conver is Type II (Papesse/Pope present); Besancon replaces them with Juno/Jupiter for Protestant markets.
Wirth took the Marseille trump sequence and iconographic program as his structural foundation, then overlaid Levi's Kabbalistic attributions.
Wirth (Paris, 1889) and the Golden Dawn (London, 1888-1900) represent parallel contemporaneous esoterization of the tarot. Both worked from Levi; both used Kabbalistic attributions.

Waite was aware of Wirth's work. Wirth established the model of a tarot where esoteric attributions are visually integrated into the card designs — the approach Waite and Smith then extended to the Minor Arcana.

The Geoffroy 1557 Lyon deck established the Marseille Type I iconographic blueprint that Parisian cardmakers adapted by c. 1600. The shift from Lyon to Paris as the northern French cardmaking center was underway in the late 16th century.
The c. 1600 Parisian fragments belong to the same Parisian cardmaking tradition that Noblet would consolidate c. 1650 into the first well-documented Paris-pattern Marseille deck.

Dodal's Marseille printing (c. 1701–1715) refines and standardizes the Paris-pattern Marseille Type II iconography that Noblet's c. 1650 deck established. The Dodal is the first full extant exemplar of the Marseille tradition that would run through Conver.

Papus's Goulinat plates for 'Le Tarot des Bohémiens' adapt Wirth's 1889 Major Arcana directly. Both projects were commissioned within the same Rosicrucian/Martinist milieu (Stanislas de Guaita was the connecting figure). The lemniscate Magician, the Kabbalistic correspondences, and several compositional choices are shared.

Waite was fluent in the French occultist tarot literature including Papus's work. While Waite explicitly distanced himself from the French Martinist system in his 'Pictorial Key to the Tarot' (1910), the underlying Lévi-derived Kabbalistic structure he shared with Papus is visible in both decks' Hebrew letter attributions and Major Arcana correspondences.

Both Sforza court commissions from the Lombard painted tradition; the Brambilla group post-dates the core VS by 30–80 years and shows stylistic refinement consistent with a later Bembo-workshop or successor-workshop commission.

The Viéville (c. 1643–1664) is a Paris-guild deck working contemporaneously with the Lyon/Marseille tradition that descends from the Geoffroy 1557. Both are mid-17th-century French woodblock traditions but from different cities and iconographic sources.

The Noblet (c. 1650) and Viéville (c. 1643–1664) are the two major surviving Paris-tradition woodblock tarots, produced in the same city and era by different cardmakers. They share the Paris guild context but differ significantly in iconographic choices — most dramatically in the Moon card.

De Gébelin most likely encountered and wrote about a Marseille Type II deck similar to the Conver 1761. The Conver is the canonical Type II surviving from this period; de Gébelin's essay is the first extended analysis of a Marseille-type tarot.

Etteilla (Jean-Baptiste Alliette) explicitly built his cartomantic system on de Gébelin's 1781 Egyptian-origin claim. De Gébelin's essay provided the intellectual authority Alliette needed to market tarot as an ancient Egyptian mystical text rather than a gaming deck.

The Lismon Grand Etteilla II is a commercial piracy of Alliette's 1789–1791 system, produced after his death. The card numbering, keyword tradition, and pseudo-Egyptian imagery are preserved with minor simplifications. Represents the commercial longevity of Alliette's cartomantic invention.

The Comte de Mellet's 1781 essay (in the same volume as de Gébelin) introduced the 22 trumps ↔ 22 Hebrew letters attribution. This was the seed that grew into Eliphas Levi's synthesis (1855), then into the Golden Dawn 'Book T' (1888). The Golden Dawn is the systematized scholarly refinement of de Mellet's original suggestion.

The Cary Sheet derives from the same Lombard/Milanese workshop tradition that produced the Visconti-Sforza hand-painted luxury decks — but represents the transition to mass-produced woodblock printing. Iconographic continuity is strong; material technique is the point of divergence.

Several Cary Sheet trump compositions — most notably The Moon and The Star — already show the Marseille Type II conventions by c. 1500, nearly 200 years before Dodal's print. The Cary Sheet is the earliest surviving evidence that the Marseille iconographic program existed as a printed tradition well before the canonical Marseille decks.

Both derive from the Lombard trump-tradition but diverge structurally: the tarocchino removes the 2–5 pips of all four suits, creating a 62-card game distinct from the 78-card Visconti/Marseille line. Mitelli's engraved Bolognese edition of 1664 is the earliest fine-art representation of this parallel Italian tradition.

Lévi explicitly built on de Gébelin's Egyptian-origin claim and de Mellet's 22-trumps-to-22-Hebrew-letters suggestion. But Lévi replaced the vague Egyptian framing with a systematic Kabbalistic one, mapping the trumps to the Tree of Life's 22 paths. This is the single most consequential transformation in the history of esoteric tarot.

Lévi's textual descriptions of The Chariot, The Magician, and The Wheel of Fortune match Marseille Type II iconography consistent with the Conver edition. Lévi treated the Marseille images as authentic documents of the (purported) ancient Egyptian original, then reinterpreted them through Kabbalah. The Conver or a closely related Marseille Type II is the most likely physical reference he consulted.

Paul Christian (Jean-Baptiste Pitois) was a close reader of Lévi and extended Lévi's Kabbalistic Egyptian frame into a full narrative of initiation. Where Lévi was abstract and systematic, Christian was narrative and evocative — but the underlying 22-trump structure is identical. Christian added the 'Major Arcana' and 'Minor Arcana' terminology that now seems native to tarot but was his invention.

Lévi is the primary source the Golden Dawn founders (Mathers, Westcott, Woodman) drew from when composing 'Book T' c. 1888. The GD tarot curriculum is essentially Lévi's system refined with the Cipher Manuscripts' additional attributions and formalized into degree-based initiation work. The previous direct-ancestor edge from de Gébelin to GD is mediated through this Lévi node — not bypassed.

The Golden Dawn adopted Paul Christian's 'Major Arcana' / 'Minor Arcana' terminology wholesale. Christian's Egyptian initiation narrative also shaped the GD's ritual framing of the trumps as stations of an inner temple — a direct literary lineage that is rarely acknowledged in GD sources but is textually obvious.

Wirth was directly commissioned by Stanislas de Guaita to produce a deck implementing Lévi's system visually. Wirth's 22 trumps are the first tarot deck printed explicitly to embody Lévi's 22-letters-and-22-paths framework. The lemniscate on The Magician, the specific Baphomet form of The Devil, and the Hebrew-letter placement all trace directly to Lévi.

The 1JJ Swiss is the 19th-century commercial codification of the Protestant-region Juno/Jupiter substitutions pioneered by the Tarot de Besançon tradition from c. 1650 onward. Müller & Cie institutionalized the substitutions into a continuously-printed product that outlived both Besançon proper and most other regional Marseille variants.

B.O.T.A. line-art cards are derivative of Pamela Colman Smith's RWS compositions with doctrinal modifications per Case's revised Qabalistic system. The relationship is not reaction-against but direct pedagogical extension: Case considered RWS a correct starting point that needed Qabalistic refinement rather than wholesale replacement (which was Crowley's view).

Case transmitted the Golden Dawn curriculum via his Alpha et Omega membership and subsequent B.O.T.A. founding. The B.O.T.A. system is the major American inheritance of the GD tradition, distinct from the English RWS/Waite line and from Crowley's Thelemic Thoth line. Case's modifications (e.g., The Emperor / The Star Hebrew-letter swap) reflect his own readings of the Cipher Manuscripts rather than Waite's.
PMB is a third Bembo-circle Milanese deck, distinct from but stylistically continuous with Visconti-Sforza. Both descend from the same Cremona/Milan Bembo-workshop environment.
PMB (luxury hand-painted) and Cary Sheet (mass-produced woodblock) are near-contemporary witnesses to the stabilization of Milanese tarot iconography c.1500.
Cary and Rosenwald sheets together are the two primary witnesses to early printed Italian tarot; both date to c.1500 and preserve the canonical Milanese/Order-A trump sequence.
Steele Sermon records the trump order in writing c.1495; Cary and Rosenwald sheets instantiate that order in printed imagery c.1500.
Rosenwald trump sheet ordering matches the Steele Sermon's 'Order A' Milanese sequence, providing image-plus-text confirmation of the canonical pre-Marseille trump sequence.
Ferrarese Este commissions represent a third major 15th c. tarot production center alongside the Milanese Visconti-lineage decks, proving early tarot was cross-regional.
The Ferrara-Este and Sola-Busca (also Ferrarese attribution) decks together establish a distinct Emilian iconographic lineage parallel to the Milanese Visconti tradition.

Steele Sermon's trump order matches the implied ordering of the Visconti-Sforza trumps (where extant), establishing that the canonical Milanese/Order-A sequence was shared between luxury and documentary traditions.

Noblet's Paris Type I Marseille (c.1650) informs but does not directly copy the Dijon Type II tradition Madenié represents (1709). Both derive from the broader 17th c. French tarot workshop environment.
Madenié (Dijon, 1709) and Dodal (Lyon, c.1701–1715) are near-contemporary Type II Marseille exemplars sharing the canonical iconographic program that Conver 1761 later propagates.

Conver's 1761 Marseille is typographically and iconographically closest to the Madenié 1709 line, confirming Madenié as the definitive early 18th c. anchor for the Type II Marseille canon Conver then propagates globally.
Paul Marteau's 1930 Grimaud Marseille is a direct line-drawing and palette adaptation of the Conver-lineage Marseille tradition, produced for 20th c. French commercial distribution.
Palladini's Aquarian preserves Smith's scenic pip compositions and reworks the trumps in Art Nouveau/Deco idiom, establishing the post-RWS 'illustrated art deck' template.
Dowson's Hermetic Tarot is a synthetic reconstruction of the Golden Dawn ritual-paper imagery, the most faithful GD-tradition deck after the Thoth.

The Hermetic borrows some Crowley-Harris decisions (e.g., the GD court rank structure Princess/Prince/Queen/Knight) while departing from Harris's Deco abstraction in favor of dense GD-ritualist linework.

Motherpeace retains the 78-card / 22-trump / 4-suit RWS structural skeleton while replacing nearly every iconographic and symbolic choice with reconstructed pre-patriarchal goddess imagery — the founding precedent for the post-RWS structural-reframe tradition.

Crowley absorbed Lévi's Dogme et Rituel de la Haute Magie thoroughly. The Kabbalistic-astrological-Hebrew letter attribution framework that underlies the Thoth deck derives ultimately from Lévi's schema (transmitted through the Golden Dawn). Crowley corrects, extends, and disputes Lévi throughout The Book of Thoth — an engagement that reveals how directly he was reading him.

Harris's paintings and Crowley's text were produced simultaneously (1938–1943/1944) as a unified system. The text is the interpretive key to the deck; neither is complete without the other. Published together by Weiser in 1969. Crowley directed Harris's painting choices based on the same doctrinal content that appears in the book.

The Hebrew letter attributions, astrological correspondences, and Kabbalistic Tree of Life structure in The Book of Thoth derive from the unpublished Golden Dawn manuscripts Crowley was initiated into. Crowley extends the GD system with Thelemic innovations (the Aeon of Horus doctrine, Liber AL correspondences) but the structural skeleton is GD material.

The Pictorial Key was written by Waite as the authorised interpretive guide to the RWS deck, published within a year of the deck itself. They were designed as a pair: the deck encodes the symbolism, the Key discloses (partially) what it means. The same publisher (Rider & Co.) produced both.

The Key's symbolic system derives from the Golden Dawn curriculum. Waite's Hebrew letter attributions, Kabbalistic correspondences, and elemental assignments all come from GD manuscripts. The Key then partially translates this material for a non-initiated audience, while carefully omitting the portions Waite considered oath-bound.

Two direct structural dependencies: (1) The Aeon card's entire iconography — the three divine figures Nuit, Hadit, Ra-Hoor-Khuit — derives from the three-chapter structure of Liber AL. (2) The Tzaddi swap (I:57: 'Tzaddi is not the Star') is Crowley's sole stated authority for reassigning Hebrew letters to The Star (major-17) and The Emperor (major-04). Without Liber AL there is no Aeon card and no Tzaddi swap — the two most structurally radical features of the Thoth deck.

The Book of Thoth is in large part an extended commentary on Liber AL's cosmological system as applied to the 78 cards. Crowley cites Liber AL throughout; the Aeon chapter (Part Two, Chapter XX) is essentially an exegesis of the divine triad. The Book of Thoth cannot be understood without Liber AL as its doctrinal foundation.

Crowley engaged Lévi's Dogme et Rituel throughout The Book of Thoth — disputing his attributions, correcting his Hebrew, and building on his foundational claim that the tarot encodes Kabbalistic wisdom. The Book of Thoth is in part a correction and completion of Lévi's project: Lévi sketched the Kabbalistic skeleton; Crowley built full architecture on it, extending with Thelema, I Ching, and his own GD initiatory experience.

Lévi opens Dogme et Rituel de la Haute Magie (1854) by explicitly engaging and repudiating Etteilla's card attribution system. Etteilla had reassigned the Hebrew letters to the Majors according to his own cartomantic logic — a sequence that Lévi found arbitrary and occultly ungrounded. Lévi's alternative assignment (Aleph = I/The Juggler, Bet = II/The High Priestess, etc.) was his counter-proposal, and Lévi's system — not Etteilla's — is what the Golden Dawn, Waite, and Crowley all inherited. This reaction-against edge is the fork in the road: after Lévi, there are two distinct tarot traditions — the Etteilla cartomantic lineage (Grand Etteilla → Etteilla II → 19th-century French cartomancy) and the Lévi esoteric lineage (Lévi → GD → RWS → Thoth). The two lineages rarely interact after this point.

Gérard Encausse (Papus, 1865–1916) was Lévi's most systematic French successor. His Tarot des Bohémiens (1889) explicitly presents itself as a rigorous elaboration of Lévi's Kabbalistic framework applied to the 78-card tarot. Papus accepts Lévi's 22-Major/22-Hebrew-letter doctrine, adopts his planetary and elemental correspondences, and extends Lévi's system into a complete divinatory manual. Where Lévi was often gestural and provocative, Papus was systematic and teacherly — his deck and text became the primary vector through which Lévi's ideas reached late 19th-century French occultist circles. Papus was also a founding member of the Ordre Martiniste and in contact with the Golden Dawn's Paris Ahathoor temple — making him a transmission point between the French and English esoteric traditions.

Papus drew directly on Paul Christian's Egyptian temple pseudo-narrative as the structuring frame for the Major Arcana interpretation in Tarot des Bohémiens. Christian had described the 22 Majors as 22 initiatory stations in a secret Egyptian temple — numbered explicitly from 1 to 22. Papus accepted this numbered sequence and the Egyptian initiation framework (while knowing it was a fabrication) as a useful pedagogical myth. Christian's Egyptian pseudo-names for the Majors (Le Mage, La Porte du Sanctuaire, La Reine du Ciel, etc.) appear in Papus's text. The transmission of Christian's numbering scheme through Papus was one route by which the modern numbered Major Arcana sequence became standardised before the Golden Dawn manuscripts circulated.
Morgan-Greer preserves the RWS sequence, scenic Minor Arcana, and positional logic while replacing Smith's visual treatment with Bill Greer's borderless, saturated compositions.
Universal Waite is a direct RWS edition with Mary Hanson-Roberts's recoloring and updated commercial reproduction.
Robin Wood retains the RWS narrative structure while recasting its scenes through pagan, Celtic, and nature-centered imagery.
The Camoin-Jodorowsky restoration presents itself as a recovery of the Marseille tradition and relies especially on Conver-lineage details alongside comparisons with other historical exemplars.
The Wild Unknown follows the familiar 78-card RWS-compatible architecture while replacing most human scenes with animal, botanical, and geometric symbolism.
Light Seer's Tarot retains RWS positions and card narratives while translating them into contemporary psychological and spiritual imagery.
Modern Witch Tarot is an explicitly contemporary RWS reinterpretation, retaining the sequence and core scenes while changing setting, bodies, and social context.
